# AGENTS.md

Read [docs/README.md](docs/README.md) first. It is the task router. Read the
owning feature's `AGENTS.md` and only the relevant implementation documentation.
Do not preload the documentation tree or invent another architecture.

## Implementation ownership

- `app/`: thin Expo Router entrypoints, route/layout declarations and metadata.
- `features/`: product presentation, domain state/actions, services, rules and tests.
- `runtime/`: cross-feature state and lifecycle composition. One application owner,
  one connection owner, and retained connection/project branches preserve continuity.
- `shared/`: feature-independent controls, contracts, protocol, platform, storage,
  query infrastructure, i18n and utilities.
- `modules/`: native Expo modules; preserve discovery and registered module names.
- `tests/e2e/` and `tests/fake-opencode/`: the behavioral contract, with central harnesses.

See [feature boundaries](docs/architecture/feature-boundaries.md) for ownership,
public APIs and the strictly limited shared UI/runtime exception.

## Start here

| Task touches | Read before editing | Validate with |

| Copy/translations | [Translations recipe](docs/engineering/task-recipes.md#translations) | `npm run gen:i18n`, strict i18n test |
| Settings or reusable UI | [Settings recipe](docs/engineering/task-recipes.md#settings-section-or-row), [design system](docs/design/design-system.md), owning component inventory | Storybook and affected E2E |

## Boundary rules

Keep domain state out of routes and presentation. Settings and Onboarding may
compose public UI from other features; that does not transfer state ownership.

Use a feature's named `index.ts`, `context.ts` or `runtime.ts` exports across
features. Inside a feature, import its implementation directly. Do not add private
cross-feature imports, wildcard public exports, cycles, parallel component copies
or compatibility shims. `config/architecture.json` is the enforced edge/export
policy; keep its changes deliberate and documented.

Presentation never fetches, persists credentials, normalizes raw server payloads,
or directly invokes arbitrary native SDKs. Reuse domain actions, pure contracts
and the shared platform interfaces. Shared UI remains feature-independent. Only
the exact existing controls listed in the architecture documentation may import
specified symbols from `runtime/ui.ts`; no new bridge context or duplicated state.

Protocol normalization belongs in `shared/protocol/`. Existing V1 imports and
compatibility branching stay in the compatibility/contract boundary. New
API-dependent features are V2-only; never add a new V1 adapter or fallback.

Preserve the single connectivity/query owners, connection-wide catalogs/streams,
credential-generation guards, retained workspace state and stable presentation map.
Do not mirror Query responses into another state store. Preserve SSE plus polling,
foreground/demand gates and the separation between inspection, terminal and chat focus.

Native changes also follow [native module guidance](modules/AGENTS.md) and
[ADR 0016](docs/adr/0016-supported-expo-native-integrations.md). Keep Expo MCP
optional and out of normal CI; do not vendor generic skills or update unrelated
dependencies during SDK migrations.

## Ratchets and UI foundation

- The provider entrypoint stays at most 60 lines; production source files at most 500.
- Combined domain-context surface stays at or below 127 members. Do not raise limits.
- Fix layering failures by moving code to its owner, not by adding broad exceptions.
- Preserve keyboard avoidance, tab layout, native modal hosts, workspace scope,
  keyboard/Back behavior, localization, text scaling and specialized renderers.
- Read [ADR 0013](docs/adr/0013-source-owned-ui-and-complex-forms.md) before UI
  foundation changes. Use the source-owned controls in `shared/ui/`, CVA and `cn()`.
- Author tokens only in `shared/ui/theme/ui-tokens.json`; run `npm run gen:ui-tokens`
  and check mode. No new styling engine, Paper wrappers or generic form framework.
- Complex forms use existing React Hook Form/Zod validators. Simple preferences
  remain immediate. Registry upgrades are reviewed source diffs with provenance.
- Reusable presentation changes need a colocated production-component Storybook
  story and `npm run build:storybook`; see [Storybook](docs/design/storybook.md); orchestration/full screens belong in E2E.

## Architecture Decision Records

Follow [the ADR process](docs/adr/README.md): copy the numbered template, update the index and link the decision from its implementation document. Supersede accepted ADRs without rewriting their reasoning.

## Development loop

1. Find the owner through the router and scoped guidance; extend existing code.
2. Make the smallest complete change, preserving error handling and trust validation.
3. Update behavior coverage at the cheapest sufficient level. Existing coverage is
   sufficient for behavior-preserving moves; explain that in the PR.
4. Add every new/changed user-facing string to every supported locale under
   `shared/i18n/locales/`, retaining placeholders/plurals. Run `npm run gen:i18n`
   and strict parity checks. English runtime fallback is not completion.
5. Update current implementation docs and section README links in the same change.
6. Record durable decisions with an ADR; supersede accepted decisions, never rewrite them.
7. Run the commit gate below, then push to `main` or update the PR branch, and
   inspect GitHub Actions. Fix failures there. CI is the final integration authority;
   it is not the first validator.

## Commit gate

Every commit, including documentation-only and follow-up fix commits, must pass
the local commit gate before it is created or amended:

1. Run `npm run validate:commit`.
2. Run the owning focused checks from the task router and
   [test-selection matrix](docs/engineering/validation/strategy.md#test-selection-matrix).
   Protocol/fake-server changes also run `npm run test:fake-server:self`; UI flow
   changes run the affected Playwright spec; localization changes run
   `npm run gen:i18n` and the strict i18n test.
3. If a required command fails, or the toolchain cannot run it (wrong Node
   version, missing package manager, missing browser), do not commit. Fix the
   toolchain or ask for help. CI is not a substitute for a local check.
4. Never commit "to see what CI says" after a preventable local failure. Do not
   amend a commit to hide a failed gate; fix the failure and rerun the gate.
5. Report the exact commands and outcomes in the final summary. State any check
   that could not run and why. "I could not run the tests" blocks the commit.

## Validation

Baseline for touched code: `npm run validate:commit`. Feature tests are
colocated; `tests/vitest/test-discovery.test.ts` prevents suites silently disappearing
from Vitest or TypeScript. Do not increase the test-typecheck exclusion budget.

`ci.yml` runs static checks, Vitest/architecture, fake-server validation, Storybook,
FOSS preparation and critical Playwright smoke flows on every push to `main` and every
PR. `release.yml` runs the full browser E2E suite and native release builds once on a
`v*` tag. `android-cache.yml` rebuilds the Android release tasks twice a week so
`release.yml` can restore a warm Gradle build cache; it publishes nothing. Use the
[test-selection matrix](docs/engineering/validation/strategy.md#test-selection-matrix)
to choose focused local checks; the full suite is not a per-push requirement.

A red CI run blocks merge. Confirm and harden flaky failures instead of adding retries.
Native/Android-risk changes may be checked locally with `npm run build:development:android`
when an SDK is available, but the tag release is the authoritative native build. Play
internal testing and TestFlight are the real-device validation environments. Static
release verification cannot guarantee successful device startup.

Any edit under `tests/e2e/` or `tests/fake-opencode/` requires explicit human validation
even when automation passes. Do not add E2E specs when existing owning specs or
lower-level tests suffice; update the budget in the same change when intentionally
adding browser coverage.

For iteration, use `validate:fast`, `test:e2e:smoke` or `test:e2e:last-failed`.
Concurrent runs use `test:e2e:web:isolated`; preserve per-worker backend isolation.

## Release

Android release artifacts are `arm64-v8a` only; 32-bit-only Android devices are
unsupported. Do not add `armeabi-v7a`, `x86` or `x86_64` to a release build.

For every release version increase:

1. Update `version`, `android.versionCode` and `ios.buildNumber` in `app.config.ts`.
2. Update the matching `package.json` version.
3. Add `fastlane/metadata/android/en-US/changelogs/<versionCode>.txt`.
4. Commit to `main`, then create and push the `v<version>` tag.

GitHub Actions performs validation, signing, Google Play internal upload, TestFlight upload
and GitHub Release publication. Do not run manual packaging, signing, upload or release
scripts. Never move or delete a release tag; fix forward with a new version. A failed
release validation is not a reason to move the tag: bump the version, commit the fix,
and tag the new commit.

A local temporary mirror may run heavy checks. Make every source edit here, sync
before checking, treat mirror output as read-only, and never commit/tag/push there.
Run generators that update committed files here. Exclude AppleDouble `._*` metadata
from mirrors; preserve nested native/fastlane Android directories.

For every release version increase, add concise release notes in
`fastlane/metadata/android/en-US/changelogs/<android.versionCode>.txt` matching
`app.config.ts`, and include the changelog in the release commit.

A change is done when ownership, behavior, localization, docs/ADRs, stories,
validation and required human checks are satisfied. The final summary states what
changed, what passed and any remaining risk.

# features/

Start with the owning feature's `AGENTS.md` and [docs router](../docs/README.md).
[Feature boundaries](../docs/architecture/feature-boundaries.md) defines the common
layout, runtime ownership, shared interfaces and enforced import policy.

Use `index.ts` for public consumer UI/types, `context.ts` for existing domain
subscriptions and `runtime.ts` for headless orchestration. Inside a feature, use
its implementation directly. Do not add cycles or private cross-feature imports.
Keep generic controls in shared UI and domain-specific preference fields here.
Runtime mounts domain state; screens never become another shared owner.

Colocate Vitest tests in colocated __tests__/ directories and stories with reusable components. Existing
Playwright flows and fake-server fixtures remain central. Follow the risk-based
validation matrix; CI is the integration authority and the tag release runs the full gate.

# Native modules

Read the [native integration reference](../docs/engineering/integrations-and-operations.md)
and [ADR 0017](../docs/adr/0017-native-defaults-and-prebuilt-engines.md).

Use SDK-compatible Expo APIs first. A local Expo module needs a documented missing
capability; preserve module discovery, registered names, service/task identities
and FOSS exclusions. Keep product policy in its feature and JS native access in
`shared/platform/`. Do not initialize models, microphones or services at import.

Clean up listeners and resources at their existing lifetime. Preserve the
content-capture mitigation immediately after `super.onCreate(null)`; an Activity
listener runs inside the superclass path and is not an equivalent replacement.
Never edit generated native projects as a durable implementation.

Keep Llama on an exact version with matching upstream engine prebuilts. Never
set `rnllamaBuildFromSource=true` or `RNLLAMA_BUILD_FROM_SOURCE=1`, or bypass a
source-only release's restriction with stale binaries. The existing JNI/ObjC
binding still compiles normally. See the [compatibility decision](../docs/engineering/library-extraction.md#local-classifier-compatibility).

Use existing build scripts and the [validation matrix](../docs/engineering/validation/strategy.md).
Debug builds and web tests do not certify R8, permissions, signing or store behavior.

# runtime/

Read [state and data](../docs/architecture/state-and-data.md#state-ownership-overview)
and [feature boundaries](../docs/architecture/feature-boundaries.md).

## Ownership

- `runtime/workspace/workspace-provider.tsx`: registry/focus, root persistence coordination,
  native coordinators, and the single connectivity monitor.
- `runtime/connections/connection-runtime.tsx`: one connection lifecycle/catalog owner.
- `runtime/workspace/workspace-runtime.tsx`: retained connection/project branch.
- `runtime/composition/`: domain wiring, values, reset and cross-feature effects.
- `runtime/persistence/`: app hydration/write-back and cross-domain credential-scope migration.
- `runtime/realtime/`: SSE plus polling reconciliation and coalescing.
- `runtime/presentation/`: stable drafts/scroll positions, independent of registry updates.

Use feature headless APIs for behavior; do not grow domain logic in composition.
Preserve query partitions, cancellation, foreground/demand gates, explicit readiness,
connection-wide catalogs/streams, and independent Settings/Terminal/Chat targets.
Keep one owner per value and the existing provider/context ordering.

`ui.ts` exports only the existing workspace scope/context and update-blocker hook.
Its value imports must never reach root composition, mounts or feature presentation.
No bridge context, state duplication or broader shared UI exception is allowed.

Validate with runtime Vitest, architecture/discovery checks and the owning E2E flows.
The tag release runs full E2E; browser/fake-server edits need human validation.

# shared/

Read [feature boundaries](../docs/architecture/feature-boundaries.md). Shared code
provides contracts/infrastructure used across product domains; it never imports a
feature. Keep protocol normalization, credential storage and native device resources
in their existing owners. Do not mirror domain state here or introduce new stores.
The only upward dependency is the exact existing UI-control allowlist for `runtime/ui`.
Run colocated shared tests and the root validation matrix; protocol/storage/query
changes require the complete gate.

# OpenCode Mobile

Your OpenCode workflow, in your pocket.

Start tasks, check progress, review changes, use the terminal, speak follow-ups, and manage OpenCode workspaces from Android and iOS.

Website · Docs · Support

--- ## OpenCode, without being tied to your laptop OpenCode Mobile is an independent, community-built mobile companion for [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/). It connects to the OpenCode server you already run and gives you a focused mobile control surface for the moments when you need to check, guide, approve, or continue agent work away from your desk. It is not trying to put a desktop IDE on a smaller screen. It is designed around the things that actually matter on mobile.

## Documentation rules

- **Update docs in the same change as the behavior.** A code change that alters
  architecture, behavior, a protocol, a user flow, or a design contract is not
  complete until the matching doc is updated.
- **Record decisions in ADRs.** If a change selects an approach, changes a
  boundary, or rejects a viable alternative, add an ADR under `docs/adr/`.
  Do not bury the reason in a code comment or a pull-request description.
- **Keep one source of truth.** Do not duplicate full command lists, endpoint
  tables, or token values across docs. Task recipes may name only the commands
  that task needs; link to the owning page for the rest.
- **Keep the router current.** Every doc must be reachable from this page or a
  section README. `tests/vitest/docs.test.ts` enforces links and ADR shape.
- **Use relative links.** Link to files with relative Markdown links so the
  tree stays portable.
- **State status.** Proposals and deferred work must say so near the top;
  implementation docs describe shipped behavior.
- **Keep it lean.** Remove historical validation logs, duplicated narratives,
  and local artifact paths instead of archiving them. If a fact is encoded in a
  test or spec, link to the owner rather than repeating it.
- **ADRs are immutable.** Once accepted, an ADR is never rewritten; supersede it
  with a new record and update the index.

## Scope notes

- This documentation covers the mobile app implementation, not OpenCode server
  internals.
- Descriptions are based on the source code and deterministic fake-server
  fixtures in this repository.
- Platform-dependent behavior is described exactly, including limitations.
- Visual acceptance evidence belongs in the pull request or design review, not
  in a committed historical log. It is not a substitute for physical-device,
  screen-reader, or store acceptance.

# F-Droid submission

This directory holds the material for submitting OpenCode Mobile's de-Googled
FOSS build to the **main F-Droid repository**. There is no self-hosted F-Droid
repo; users install either from F-Droid or from the `opencode-mobile-fdroid.apk`
asset on GitHub releases.

See [`docs/engineering/fdroid.md`](../docs/engineering/fdroid.md) for how the FOSS variant is produced.

## Submitting to fdroiddata

1. Ensure the upstream source commit contains the FOSS support and complete
   `en-US` Fastlane metadata. Keep the Firebase stub revision in the FOSS build
   script and the template's `firebase-stub` srclib in sync.
   Releases use `v*` tags; the `foss-release` CI job attaches the FOSS APK.
2. Fork and clone [fdroiddata](https://gitlab.com/fdroid/fdroiddata).
3. Copy `fdroiddata/app.getopencode.fdroid.yml` into the fork at
   `metadata/app.getopencode.fdroid.yml`, and set `commit:` to that release's
   full source commit SHA. If metadata or build support was added after the
   release tag, pin the merged upstream main commit containing those fixes.
   Verify the SHA exists in a fresh clone. Rebase/squash merges rewrite commit
   hashes, so a pre-merge topic-branch SHA can become unavailable to F-Droid.
4. Decide the signing approach before first publication. Reproducible builds
   are currently not enabled; the reasons are recorded in `MaintainerNotes`
   and [`docs/engineering/fdroid.md`](../docs/engineering/fdroid.md). Only after unsigned APK equivalence
   has been verified should you enable `Binaries`/`AllowedAPKSigningKeys` or
   extract upstream signatures:
   ```bash
   curl -L -o opencode-mobile-fdroid.apk \
      https://github.com/alvarolorentedev/opencode-mobile/releases/download/v1.0.55/opencode-mobile-fdroid.apk
   fdroid signatures opencode-mobile-fdroid.apk
   ```
   Place the extracted files under
   `metadata/app.getopencode.fdroid/signatures/<versionCode>/`.
5. Validate:
   ```bash
   fdroid checkupdates --allow-dirty app.getopencode.fdroid
   fdroid lint app.getopencode.fdroid
   fdroid build app.getopencode.fdroid
   ```
6. Keep the fork public and the source branch unprotected. Use the MR title
   `New app: OpenCode Mobile`, include the checklist and reproducibility
   explanation, and submit only `metadata/app.getopencode.fdroid.yml`.
   F-Droid maintainers review, build, and publish it.

## Reviewer notes

- The FOSS build excludes Google Play Billing and ML Kit barcode scanning and
  compiles `expo-notifications` against F-Droid's `firebase-stubs` rather than
  Firebase Cloud Messaging. Local notifications still work.
- Voice input uses the device's system speech recognizer; if reviewers apply
  `NonFreeNet`, declare it in the recipe rather than dropping the feature.

# Architecture Decision Records

ADRs capture decisions that are expensive to reverse or that shape how future
changes are made. They explain **why** the code is the way it is. The rest of
`docs/` explains **what** the code does.

## When to write an ADR

Write one when a change:

- selects a framework, transport, storage model, or protocol boundary
- changes ownership between `app/`, `components/`, `providers/`, `lib/`, or
  `providers/services/`
- adds or removes a compatibility path or a supported platform
- establishes a design-system primitive, token family, or accessibility policy
- rejects a viable alternative for a reason future maintainers need to know
- changes the documentation or decision workflow itself

Do not write an ADR for a routine bug fix, a local refactor that preserves
boundaries, or a copy change. If you are unsure, ask whether a future
maintainer would otherwise re-litigate the choice.

## Workflow

1. Copy [template.md](template.md) to
   `docs/adr/NNNN-short-kebab-title.md`, using the next four-digit number.
2. Fill in context, decision, consequences, and alternatives. Keep it short and
   concrete; link to code and docs instead of duplicating them.
3. Add the ADR to the index below in the same change.
4. Link the ADR from the affected implementation doc and mention it in the
   change summary.
5. If a later decision replaces it, set the old status to `Superseded by ADR
   NNNN` and add the new ADR. Do not rewrite history.

`tests/vitest/docs.test.ts` checks ADR numbering, required sections, index
coverage, and documentation links.

## Status values

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Proposed` | Under discussion; not yet binding |
| `Accepted` | Current decision |
| `Superseded by ADR NNNN` | Replaced; kept for history |
| `Deprecated` | No longer recommended, but not directly replaced |
| `Rejected` | Considered and declined |

How the app is composed, where state lives, and how it talks to OpenCode.

transport, persistence, or the client protocol. Read

## Documents

| Document | Owns |

| [feature-boundaries.md](feature-boundaries.md) | Product ownership, public APIs, exact scope-aware UI exception and migration inventory |

## Where does this live?

| Concern | Owning layer |
| --- | --- |
| App-wide connection registry, focus, and persistence | `runtime/workspace/workspace-provider.tsx`, `runtime/workspace/use-workspace-connections.ts`, `runtime/persistence/use-opencode-persistence.ts` |
| Provider-specific agent guidance | `runtime/AGENTS.md` (loaded when working in `runtime/`) |
| Routine server reads and connection lifecycle | `shared/server-data/`, `runtime/connections/connection-runtime.tsx` ([ADR 0014](../adr/0014-server-data-and-explicit-lifecycles.md)) |
| Per-workspace domain orchestration | `runtime/composition/use-opencode-provider-composition.ts` and its domain hooks |
| Public domain contexts and hooks | `shared/contracts/domain.ts`, `features/chat/context.ts`, `runtime/workspace/domain-provider-tree.tsx` |
| Provider-facing API aggregation | `shared/protocol/services/` |
| Client construction, endpoint wrappers, protocol types | `shared/protocol/opencode/` |
| V1 compatibility only | `shared/protocol/opencode/compat/v1/` |
| Routing and thin screen wiring | `app/` |
| Presentation and local UI state | `features/` |
| Behavioral contract | `tests/fake-opencode/` and `tests/e2e/` |

## Rules

- The app is provider-centric. Domain state and orchestration belong in
  `runtime/`, not in screens or presentational components.
- Keep protocol normalization close to `shared/protocol/opencode/`.
- Preserve the dual realtime model: SSE is primary, polling is the safety net.
- New API-dependent features are V2-only unless an existing V1 compatibility
  path already supports them. See [ADR 0003](../adr/0003-v2-first-protocol-boundary.md).
- If you change a boundary, protocol, or ownership rule, add an
  [ADR](../adr/README.md) and update the relevant page here.
- `tests/vitest/architecture.test.ts` enforces the size, context-surface,
  network/persistence, and compatibility boundaries. Fix a failure by moving
  code to the right layer; do not raise the limit.

## Change checklist

1. Identify the owning layer in the table above.
2. Read the matching document and the [state and data](state-and-data.md) page.
3. Make the smallest change that preserves documented behavior.
4. Update the fake server or E2E contract if the client contract changed.
5. Update this section and record any decision in `docs/adr/`.
6. Run the validation required by `AGENTS.md`.

## Design workflow

1. **Start from the system.** Author shared values in `shared/ui/theme/ui-tokens.json`.
   Use the generated CSS and TypeScript projections in `shared/ui/theme/theme.ts`
   and `shared/ui/theme/design-tokens.ts`; appearance preferences remain in
   `shared/ui/theme/appearance.ts`. Do not duplicate tokens in components.
2. **Reuse before adding.** Check the [component inventory](component-inventory.md)
   and the matching area file before creating a new control.
3. **Build the component in its correct layer.** Presentation and local UI
   state live in `features/`; provider state and orchestration stay in
   `runtime/`. See [architecture](../architecture/README.md).
4. **Add a Storybook story** for reusable primitives and shared controls. See
   [storybook.md](storybook.md).
5. **Validate states, not just the happy path.** Cover loading, empty, disabled,
   error, success, destructive, keyboard, long translations, dark mode, accent
   presets, and narrow widths.
6. **Record visual acceptance** with the [QA template](qa/template.md) when a
   design review is part of the change; attach it to the pull request.
7. **Record design decisions** that constrain the system in an
   [ADR](../adr/README.md). A new token family, control primitive, or
   accessibility policy is a decision, not an incidental style change.

## Rules

- Use semantic palette roles through `usePalette()`; never read
  `Colors.light` directly in a component.
- Keep platform fonts. Do not add a font dependency.
- Use MaterialCommunityIcons. A trailing chevron means navigation; a switch
  changes a boolean immediately.
- Preserve accessible targets, labels, checked/expanded/disabled state, and
  visible focus.
- Do not communicate disabled state through opacity alone.
- Do not add decorative motion. Respect reduced motion.
- Every new or changed user-facing string must be translated in every supported

# Design QA

Design QA is the evidence trail for visual and interaction acceptance. It is
not a substitute for physical-device, screen-reader, or store acceptance.

## When to record a review

Record a review when a change:

- introduces or materially changes a shared visual pattern
- adds a new full-screen flow or sheet
- changes responsive, keyboard, safe-area, or large-text behavior
- changes light/dark or accent-preset presentation
- is explicitly reviewed against a design reference

Small copy or token-only changes do not need a separate report unless the
review found something worth preserving.

## Required evidence

- The selected design reference or source, with its location
- The implemented states, with viewport, density, theme, and fixture details
- The comparison method (side-by-side, live app, screenshots)
- Findings by severity (`P0`, `P1`, `P2`, `P3`) and the fix for each
- Intentional differences from the reference and why they preserve the system
- What remains unverified (native microphone, real store purchase, screen
  reader, physical device, and so on)
- The final result: `passed`, `passed with follow-ups`, or `blocked`

Use [template.md](template.md) as the starting point. Attach the completed
report to the pull request or design review. Do not commit a running log of
historical reviews or local artifact paths.

## Rules

- Do not claim screen-reader or native acceptance from screenshots.
- Do not hide unresolved P0/P1 findings behind a "passed" summary.
- Describe temporary artifacts instead of linking to local paths that do not
  exist in a clean checkout.
- A design review that changes the system itself needs an
  [ADR](../../adr/README.md).

# ADR 0001: Record architecture decisions as ADRs

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-29
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [ADR index](README.md), [documentation router](../README.md)

## Context

Architecture decisions were spread across implementation docs, pull-request
descriptions, code comments, and commit history. The implementation docs explain
what the app does, but they do not consistently explain why a boundary exists
or which alternatives were rejected. That makes it easy to re-open settled
questions, and it makes agent-assisted changes riskier because an agent can
"improve" a deliberate constraint without seeing the reason.

## Decision

Use Architecture Decision Records under `docs/adr/`.

- Every decision that changes a boundary, selects a durable approach, or
  rejects a viable alternative gets a numbered ADR.
- ADRs use the [template](template.md) and are indexed in the
  [ADR README](README.md).
- ADRs are immutable after acceptance except for status changes and links. A
  replacement decision gets a new ADR and marks the old one superseded.
- `AGENTS.md` and the documentation workflow require an ADR when the trigger
  applies.
- `tests/vitest/docs.test.ts` validates ADR numbering, required sections, and
  index coverage.

## Consequences

- Future maintainers can find the reason for a boundary without reconstructing
  it from code or chat history.
- Changes carry a small documentation cost when they make a durable choice.
- Agents have an explicit instruction to check and add ADRs, which reduces
  accidental reversals.
- The ADR set must be maintained; stale statuses are worse than no ADR.

## Alternatives considered

- **Pull-request descriptions only:** close to the change, but hard to discover
  later and often lost when the repository is mirrored.
- **A wiki:** easy to edit, but drifts from the code and is not reviewed with
  the change.
- **Code comments only:** useful for local detail, but cannot compare
  alternatives or describe system-wide consequences.
- **No formal record:** preserves speed, but repeats the current problem.

## Follow-up

- [x] Add the ADR directory, template, and index.
- [x] Add the workflow to `AGENTS.md` and the documentation router.
- [x] Add the documentation contract test.

# ADR 0002: Provider-centric domain orchestration

- Status: Superseded by ADR 0015
- Date: 2026-10-29
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Architecture overview](../architecture/overview.md), [State and data](../architecture/state-and-data.md), [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md)

## Context

The app keeps several servers, projects, and sessions alive at once. Chat,
Projects, Settings, and Terminal must preserve continuity when the user switches
tabs. The same session state feeds the transcript, diff/todo caches, permission
and question queues, notifications, widgets, and the terminal. If each screen
owned its own fetches and stores, the app would duplicate requests, diverge on
session state, and lose work when a tab unmounts.

## Decision

Use a provider-centric domain layer.

- `providers/workspace-provider.tsx` owns the connection registry, focus, and
  app-wide persistence.
- Each retained connection/project branch mounts a `WorkspaceRuntime` composed
  by `providers/use-opencode-provider-composition.ts`.
- Domain contexts expose narrow hooks (`useChat()`, `useProjects()`,
  `useConnection()`, and so on). There is no combined runtime context value.
- Screens in `app/` are thin route controllers. Components in `components/`
  own presentation and local UI state only.
- `providers/services/` aggregates provider-facing API work. `lib/opencode/`
  owns protocol shaping and client construction.
- Shared state does not move into screens, presentational components, or new
  ad-hoc stores.

## Consequences

- Session, approval, and prompt state survive tab switches and workspace
  changes.
- SSE, polling, persistence, and notification tracking have one owner.
- The provider is the highest-risk part of the app; its size and public context
  surface are ratcheted by tests and must be split by domain rather than grown
  into a god object.
- A new feature usually needs a provider hook plus a thin screen/component, not
  a new state library.

## Alternatives considered

- **Screen-local state and fetches:** simple for one screen, but duplicates
  requests and loses continuity across tabs.
- **Redux or Zustand as a second global store:** workable, but would duplicate
  the existing provider ownership and complicate SSE/persistence ordering.
- **One context per screen:** reduces re-renders locally, but makes shared
  session and approval state inconsistent.
- **Server-state library only:** does not cover the conversation state machine,
  prompt admission, terminal transports, or local persistence rules.

## Follow-up

- [x] Keep domain contexts split and memoized.
- [x] Keep the provider entrypoint thin.
- [ ] Split any further provider growth by domain, not by screen.

# ADR 0003: V2-first protocol boundary with isolated V1 compatibility

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-29
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md), [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md)

## Context

OpenCode 2 is the primary server contract, but the app still supports existing
OpenCode 1 servers for behavior that already shipped. The two contracts differ
in endpoints, pagination, transcript records, diffs, inbox delivery, provider
authentication, and event shapes. Allowing compatibility branches to spread
through providers and components would make every feature carry two code paths
and would make the V1 surface grow accidentally.

## Decision

Make OpenCode 2 the primary contract and isolate V1 compatibility.

- Native V2 operations use `@opencode/client` through the typed adapter in
  `lib/opencode/`.
- `@opencode-ai/sdk` is imported only inside `lib/opencode/compat/v1/`.
- Contract branching belongs in the typed adapter or the V1 compatibility
  layer, never in screens, components, or provider hooks.
- New capabilities that require an API surface outside the existing V1
  compatibility layer are V2-only. The UI hides or disables them on V1.
- Do not add new V1 adapters, endpoint shims, fallbacks, or fake-server handlers
  for new V2-only capabilities.
- Contract discovery probes V2 first and falls back only for missing endpoints
  or malformed protocol responses, never for authentication or transport
  failures.

## Consequences

- New features ship once, against the current contract.
- V1 remains supported for existing behavior and maintenance fixes, but its
  surface is frozen unless a deliberate decision expands it.
- Protocol normalization stays testable and close to `lib/opencode/`.
- Fake-server and E2E coverage must continue to exercise both contracts where
  behavior is shared.

## Alternatives considered

- **Implement every new feature on both contracts:** doubles the work and keeps
  the legacy surface growing.
- **Drop V1 immediately:** simplest code, but breaks existing users and
  connections.
- **Branch on contract everywhere:** local convenience, but spreads protocol
  knowledge into UI and provider code.
- **A separate V1 app:** isolates the code but duplicates the entire product.

## Follow-up

- [x] Keep V1 imports inside `lib/opencode/compat/v1/`.
- [x] Add an architecture ratchet against V1 SDK imports outside the boundary.
- [ ] Revisit the V1 support policy only through a new ADR.

# ADR 0004: SSE primary with polling fallback

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-29
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Network resilience](../architecture/network-resilience.md), [Architecture overview](../architecture/overview.md)

## Context

The app runs on mobile networks where a connection can look healthy while a
stream is stalled, a radio transition can drop the transport, or a server can
stop emitting events without closing the socket. The UI must still reconcile
session status, pending permissions and questions, transcripts, and terminal
state. Trusting a single transport would leave the app silently stale.

## Decision

Use SSE as the primary realtime transport and polling as an explicit safety net.

- One global SSE subscription per server is fanned out to retained projects and
  filtered by directory.
- Reconnects use jittered exponential backoff from 1 second to 15 seconds, with
  a first-byte/connect timeout and a stable-stream reset.
- A watchdog reconnects after 45 seconds without activity while work or a
  blocking interaction is active, or 60 seconds while idle. Keepalive frames
  count as activity.
- Polling cadence is state-driven: none while healthy and idle, 10 seconds while
  healthy and busy (15 seconds constrained), 5 seconds while degraded
  (8 seconds constrained), and paused while offline or backgrounded.
- Foregrounding performs an authoritative reconcile and cycles a stream that was
  backgrounded for 15 seconds or more.
- Offline pauses SSE retries and polling; an online transition restarts the
  stream and runs a critical reconcile.
- An uncertain mutation is reconciled, never replayed blindly.

## Consequences

- The app recovers from stalled streams and radio transitions without requiring
  a user action.
- Realtime behavior is more complex than either transport alone, so the
  reconnect, watchdog, and polling rules must stay in one provider owner.
- Polling cost is bounded by session activity and network state.
- Tests must cover both the healthy SSE path and the degraded polling path.

## Alternatives considered

- **SSE only:** lowest latency, but no recovery when the stream stalls without
  closing.
- **Polling only:** simpler and predictable, but higher latency and more
  requests during active work.
- **Custom WebSocket protocol:** more control, but adds a server contract and
  does not remove the need for reconciliation.
- **Client-side timers without server reconciliation:** hides staleness instead
  of resolving it.

## Follow-up

- [x] Keep SSE and polling in the provider realtime hook.
- [x] Document request deadlines and reconnect rules.
- [ ] Keep the fake server's stream-disconnect and polling scenarios current.

# ADR 0005: Thin routes and presentational components

- Status: Superseded by ADR 0015
- Date: 2026-10-29
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Architecture overview](../architecture/overview.md), [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md)

## Context

Mobile screens tend to accumulate fetch logic, protocol parsing, persistence,
and shared state because those are convenient to reach from a route. That makes
behavior hard to reuse across tabs, hard to test outside the navigation stack,
and easy to duplicate. The app already has a provider-centric domain layer; the
route and component layers need a clear rule to keep it that way.

## Decision

Keep routes thin and components presentational.

- `app/` owns route entrypoints, tab/layout wiring, thin screen controllers, and
  calls into `useOpencode()` domain hooks. It does not fetch, persist, normalize
  protocol payloads, or own cross-session caches.
- `components/` owns rendering and local UI state (open sheet, search query,
  draft, expanded row, and similar). It does not call APIs, persist data, or
  create shared domain state.
- Shared behavior across tabs belongs in `providers/`.
- Protocol shaping belongs in `lib/opencode/`.
- Services in `providers/services/` aggregate provider-facing requests but do
  not own app state.

## Consequences

- Screens can be rebuilt or rearranged without moving domain behavior.
- Components are easier to preview in Storybook because they do not depend on
  the network or the workspace runtime.
- Some features require an explicit provider hook before the UI can be written;
  that is intentional friction.
- Architecture ratchets can detect fetch/persistence calls and legacy SDK
  imports in the wrong layer.

## Alternatives considered

- **Feature folders with co-located state:** good locality, but duplicates the
  provider and loses cross-tab continuity.
- **Container/presenter split only at the screen level:** helps a little, but
  still allows protocol and persistence logic to leak into screens.
- **Server-state hooks in components:** convenient for reads, but bypasses the
  provider's reconciliation and persistence rules.

## Follow-up

- [x] Keep the layering rules in `AGENTS.md`.
- [x] Keep the architecture ratchet for network and persistence calls.
- [ ] Add a provider hook or service before adding a new shared behavior to a
  component.

# ADR 0006: Semantic design tokens with React Native Paper

- Status: Superseded by ADR 0013
- Date: 2026-10-29
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Design system](../design/design-system.md), [Design section](../design/README.md)

## Context

The app supports system/light/dark modes and six accent presets. Settings,
chat, projects, terminal, onboarding, and Cloud Link all need consistent
surfaces, text, borders, status colors, and control sizes. Literal colors and
one-off control styling had produced inconsistent contrast and made new themes
expensive to add. A custom component kit would duplicate accessible primitives
that already work on iOS, Android, and web.

## Decision

Use semantic design tokens with React Native Paper as the component foundation.

- `constants/theme.ts` owns semantic palette roles and platform font families.
- `constants/appearance.ts` owns theme modes and accent presets.
- `constants/paper-theme.ts` maps the palette into Paper's theme.
- `constants/design-tokens.ts` owns spacing, shape, and minimum control sizes.
- Components resolve colors through `usePalette()` and Paper components; they do
  not read `Colors.light` directly or hard-code literal colors.
- Keep platform fonts; do not add a font dependency.
- Shared settings rows and controls (`SettingSwitchRow`, `SettingSelectField`,
  `SettingButton`, `SettingTextInput`, `SettingSlider`, `SettingsDisclosure`)
  are the default building blocks for settings-like surfaces.
- Status always has text or an icon in addition to color. Disabled state keeps
  its label, accessible state, and prerequisite hint; opacity alone is not
  enough.

## Consequences

- New screens inherit theme, contrast, and control sizing automatically.
- A new color or spacing value requires a token change and a design-system
  update, not a local literal.
- Paper's platform behavior remains the baseline, so custom controls need a
  documented reason and accessible semantics.
- Visual QA must cover light/dark, accent presets, large text, narrow widths,
  and keyboard states.

## Alternatives considered

- **Tailwind or a CSS-first system:** poor fit for React Native's style model
  and Paper integration.
- **A fully custom component kit:** more control, but duplicates accessible
  primitives and increases maintenance.
- **Per-screen palettes:** fast locally, but breaks contrast and theme
  consistency.
- **A custom font family:** stronger brand control, but adds loading, fallback,
  and platform-metric risk without solving a current usability problem.

## Follow-up

- [x] Document the token sources and interaction patterns.
- [x] Add a Storybook catalog for shared primitives.
- [ ] Keep contrast tests and the design-system checklist current.

# ADR 0007: Storybook for reusable components

- Status: Superseded by ADR 0013
- Date: 2026-10-29
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Storybook guide](../design/storybook.md), [Design system](../design/design-system.md), [Component inventory](../design/component-inventory.md)

## Context

Shared controls are exercised through full app flows. Reviewing a button,
field, switch, or state treatment currently requires booting the app, connecting
to a fake server, and navigating to the right surface. That makes it hard to
review edge states (disabled, error, long translation, dark theme, narrow width)
and easy to duplicate a control because the existing one is not discoverable.
The app already runs on web through `react-native-web`, so a browser-based
catalog is feasible without adding a native dependency to the app.

## Decision

Use Storybook as the catalog for reusable presentation components.

- Storybook runs on the web with `@storybook/react-vite` and aliases
  `react-native` to `react-native-web`.
- Stories are co-located with reusable primitives and shared controls
  (`components/**/*.stories.tsx`).
- The preview provides the real appearance provider and Paper theme, with
  light/dark and accent controls.
- Stories cover reusable presentation, not provider orchestration or full
  screens. Provider-coupled surfaces remain covered by E2E flows.
- A story must render the production component, not a parallel copy.
- `npm run build:storybook` is the catalog build check. It is not part of the
  app bundle or the E2E export.

## Consequences

- Shared controls can be reviewed in isolation across themes and states.
- The catalog becomes stale if stories are not updated with the component; the
  design-system workflow requires a story for new shared primitives.
- Web-only Storybook cannot prove native behavior. Physical-device checks remain
  required for native modules, gestures, keyboard, and accessibility.
- The Storybook dependency set is development-only and does not ship in the app.

## Alternatives considered

- **Storybook for React Native on device:** closest to production, but slower to
  review and harder to automate on this repository's CI hosts.
- **No catalog:** no new dependencies, but keeps shared controls undiscoverable
  and edge states under-reviewed.
- **Screenshot-only gallery:** useful for visual review, but does not exercise
  props, state, or accessibility semantics.
- **A custom in-app gallery:** duplicates Storybook's navigation, controls, and
  docs with more maintenance.

## Follow-up

- [x] Add the web Storybook configuration and preview decorators.
- [x] Add stories for the initial shared primitives.
- [ ] Add a story when a new reusable primitive or shared control is introduced.

# ADR 0008: Documentation information architecture and checks

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-29
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Documentation router](../README.md), [ADR index](README.md), [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md)

## Context

The documentation had grown into a flat `docs/` directory with architecture,
product behavior, design, testing, release, and deferred work mixed together.
Filenames were descriptive, but there was no task-based router, no per-section
index, and no durable place for decisions. Agents and contributors had to search
the whole tree, and moving a file silently broke links. The design material was
split between `docs/design-system.md`, a root `design-qa.md`, and a
`docs/design/` folder used for a single proposal.

## Decision

Organize documentation by purpose and make discoverability enforceable.

- Top-level sections: `architecture/`, `product/`, `design/`, `engineering/`,
  and `adr/`.
- `docs/README.md` is the task-based router and links every section.
- Each section has a `README.md` with an index, ownership map, rules, and
  related links.
- Design has a dedicated section covering the design system, component
  inventory, Storybook, QA process/log, and proposals.
- Decisions live in `docs/adr/` with an index and template; the workflow is
  part of `AGENTS.md`.
- `tests/vitest/docs.test.ts` checks that every doc is reachable from a README,
  relative Markdown links resolve, and ADRs are numbered, indexed, and shaped
  correctly.
- Documentation is updated in the same change as the behavior it describes.

## Consequences

- A contributor or agent can start from a task and reach the owning page in one
  or two links.
- Moving a doc requires updating links; the docs test catches the common cases.
- The section READMEs need maintenance, but they are short and stable.
- The ADR requirement adds a small cost to durable decisions and removes a much
  larger rediscovery cost.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the flat tree and add a better index:** less churn, but the index
  becomes a long list and design/architecture/release material still mixes.
- **One folder per feature:** good for product docs, but architecture and
  engineering concerns cut across features.
- **A generated docs site only:** useful for readers, but does not fix the
  source layout or enforce links.
- **Rely on search:** works for known terms, but not for "where do I start?" or
  "which doc owns this?"

## Follow-up

- [x] Move existing docs into the new sections and update references.
- [x] Add section READMEs, the router, ADRs, and the docs test.
- [ ] Keep new docs in the narrowest correct section.

# ADR 0009: Agent-first documentation routing and drift checks

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-29
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Documentation router](../README.md), [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md), [task recipes](../engineering/task-recipes.md), [docs checks](../../tests/vitest/docs.test.ts)

## Context

The section tree and task router from ADR 0008 made the documentation
discoverable, but the always-on instructions still told every agent to read five
reference docs before starting. That is roughly 83k tokens, or about 40% of a
200k context window, before the task is identified. The same instruction was
repeated in the router's onboarding path.

The largest reference docs also had no section maps. A settings change could
require reading the full component inventory, and a validation change could
require reading the full testing history. The docs test checked Markdown links,
anchors, ADRs, and Storybook wiring, but not inline repository paths or
`npm run` scripts, so stale commands and paths survived.

Historical validation narratives and a design QA log accumulated dates, local
artifact paths, and superseded test counts. They described work already encoded
in E2E specs and feature docs, and they made agents read irrelevant history.

## Decision

Optimize the documentation for task-scoped retrieval and enforce the parts that
can drift.

- `AGENTS.md` routes by task: a compact table maps "task touches" to the owning
  doc section and the validation command. It no longer preloads the docs tree.
- The router keeps a one-time "First time in this repo" path, explicitly marked
  as onboarding rather than a per-task requirement.
- `providers/AGENTS.md` holds provider-specific ownership and pitfalls; agents
  load it lazily when working in `providers/`.
- `docs/engineering/task-recipes.md` holds four checklists for the highest-churn
  workflows: translations, settings, fake-server/E2E, and provider state.
- Mixed reference docs are split behind stable index pages:
  `docs/design/component-inventory.md` indexes `docs/design/components/*.md`,
  and `docs/engineering/testing-and-validation.md` indexes
  `docs/engineering/validation/*.md`.
- The docs test validates inline repository paths and `npm run` scripts in
  addition to links, anchors, ADRs, and Storybook wiring.
- Historical validation logs, the design QA log, duplicated narratives, and
  local artifact paths are removed. The current contract is the E2E spec plus
  the owning feature doc; deferred coverage lives in `known-gaps.md`.
- Accepted ADRs are immutable. A later decision supersedes them; it never
  rewrites them.

## Consequences

Agents can start with the router and one task row, then read one section or
recipe. The baseline context drops from roughly 86k tokens to roughly 5k before
the task doc. Mixed reference docs can be read by area without loading the rest.

The cost is maintenance: the task table, recipes, scoped provider file, and
section indexes must stay current. The docs test catches broken links, anchors,
paths, and scripts, but not stale prose; reviewers still own semantic accuracy.
Splitting reference docs adds files, but the stable index pages keep existing
links working.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the five-doc preload:** rejected because it spends most of the context
  budget before the task is known.
- **Split every large doc:** rejected as unnecessary churn; section maps and the
  two mixed-doc splits cover the measured problem.
- **Add a docs site or search service:** rejected; it adds a dependency and does
  not improve in-repo agent retrieval.
- **Vendor Expo/React Native agent skills:** rejected; the official skills are
  generic and should be installed per developer, while repo docs remain
  authoritative for architecture, fake-server, and design contracts.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Add docs-test coverage for inline paths and scripts.
- [x] Link this ADR from the router and change summary.

# ADR 0010: Risk-based validation and selective PR E2E

- Status: Superseded by ADR 0011
- Date: 2026-10-30
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Validation strategy](../engineering/validation/strategy.md), [E2E flows](../engineering/validation/e2e.md), [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md), [ADR 0018](0018-tag-driven-release-pipeline.md)

## Context

The full Playwright suite is the slowest part of validation. At the time of the
decision it contains about 170 expanded tests and takes roughly 5 minutes of
test execution on four workers, plus about 75 seconds for the web export and
job overhead. Running it on every pull request is safe but makes agent feedback
slow and duplicates work when the same commit is later validated on `main` and
again on its release tag.

The repository is public, so standard GitHub-hosted runner minutes are free.
Wall-clock latency, release reliability, and avoidable compute are still real
costs. A solo maintainer and community contributors need a gate that is fast
for routine changes but still catches shared-contract regressions before a
release.

## Decision

Select E2E coverage by risk, but keep the full suite at the integration and
release boundaries.

- Pull requests run the critical `@smoke` set plus the specs selected from the
  changed paths. Shared contracts, unknown paths, protocol/provider code,
  test infrastructure, dependencies, and build configuration run the full
  suite.
- Every code-bearing push to `main` runs the full suite. Documentation-only
  pushes run static checks only.
- Release tags must point to a commit whose full static + E2E validation
  already succeeded on `main`. A tag does not rerun the suite; an emergency
  `force_validate` input runs the complete gate instead.
- Android and FOSS release builds run in parallel after the gate; a release
  preparation job creates the GitHub Release once before both uploads.
- E2E retries remain zero. Flakes are fixed with deterministic clocks,
  readiness signals, per-test fake-server resets, and atomic assertions, not
  with retries or larger timeouts.
- The change-to-spec mapping lives in `scripts/ci/validation-map.mjs` and is
  covered by `tests/vitest/validation-selection.test.ts`. Unknown mappings
  fail safe to the full suite.
- A required `validate / gate` check normalizes the conditional jobs. A skipped
  E2E job is accepted only when the change classification selected no E2E.

## Consequences

Routine PRs get feedback in roughly 3–5 minutes instead of 8–10. Release tags
stop duplicating the full suite, and the Android/FOSS critical path is the
longer of the two builds rather than their sum. Full `main` validation remains
the backstop when a selective PR misses a cross-area regression.

The selector must be updated when a new domain or spec is added. Raising the
E2E budget in `tests/e2e/budget.json`, adding a spec file, or changing a shared
contract is an explicit review decision. The release process must wait for the
`main` validation before tagging; a tag without a green full run fails closed.

## Alternatives considered

- **Full suite on every PR:** strongest merge gate, but keeps agent feedback at
  ~10 minutes and does not address duplicate release validation.
- **Smoke-only PRs plus a periodic full run:** cheaper, but weaker than running
  the full suite on every merge to `main`; a weekly run can leave `main` broken
  for days.
- **More Playwright shards:** halves wall-clock but roughly doubles E2E compute,
  and the current four workers already saturate the four-vCPU runner.
- **Keep tag validation:** safe but duplicates the exact same SHA validation
  and false-blocks releases when a flaky test passes on `main` but fails on the
  tag.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Add selector unit tests, a fake-server reset fixture, and an E2E budget.
- [ ] Link this ADR from the change summary.

# ADR 0011: Release from green main builds, not tag pushes

- Status: Superseded by ADR 0018
- Date: 2026-10-30
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: [ADR 0010](0010-risk-based-validation-and-selective-pr-e2e.md)
- Related: [ADR 0018](0018-tag-driven-release-pipeline.md), [`.github/workflows/release.yml`](../../.github/workflows/release.yml), [Development](../engineering/development.md), [Validation strategy](../engineering/validation/strategy.md)

## Context

ADR 0010 stopped rerunning the full suite on a release tag by making the tag
workflow assert that a successful `Build` run already existed on `main` for the
same SHA. That check runs immediately when the tag workflow starts. Pushing
`main` and its tag together therefore fails the release: the `main` run is still
queued or running when the tag queries for it.

The same change moved GitHub Release creation into a `release-gate` job so the
parallel Android and FOSS uploads would not race to create it. That introduced
a second failure mode: `release-gate` depends on the tag-only `validate` job,
which is skipped; GitHub propagates skipped ancestors through `needs` even when
the intermediate job runs with `always()`. The build jobs were skipped, the run
reported success, and the Release was left published with no assets. Rerunning
failed jobs does not recover skipped dependents.

The release trigger must not depend on a different workflow run finishing, and a
release must never be published before its assets exist.

## Decision

Validation and release are separate workflows with an event-based dependency:

- `build.yml` validates pushes to `main` only. Tag pushes do not trigger it, so
  pushing `main` and its tag together is safe.
- `release.yml` triggers on `workflow_run` when `Build` completes on `main`, and
  on manual dispatch. It reads the validated `head_sha` from that event.
- A release happens only when a `v*` tag points at the validated commit. The tag
  must match the `version` in `app.config.ts`.
- The workflow verifies the exact SHA has a successful full validation, creates
  a **draft** GitHub Release once, builds Android and FOSS in parallel, attaches
  both APKs, and publishes the draft only after both uploads succeed.
- Manual dispatch takes `tag` and `publish`. It supports repairing a broken
  release and building sideload APKs without touching a Release.
- A failed or partial build leaves an unpublished draft, never a published
  release with missing assets.

The risk-based PR selection and full `main` validation from ADR 0010 remain in
force; only its release-trigger mechanism is replaced.

## Consequences

Releases no longer race validation. A maintainer can push the version bump and
its tag in either order or together. The Release workflow runs from the default
branch, so workflow fixes apply without moving a tag.

`release.yml` rebuilds on every green `main` run only long enough to resolve the
tag and no-op; there is no build cost when the version did not change. Repairing
a release means dispatching the workflow with its tag. Manual tagging remains
required: the workflow does not bump versions or create tags.

The draft-then-publish sequence means a successful workflow is the only signal
that a release is complete. The workflow is idempotent (`--clobber` uploads and
an `isDraft` check) so it can be rerun safely.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the tag trigger and poll for the main validation:** removes the
  immediate race but keeps cross-run coupling, adds a wait, and does not fix the
  skipped-dependent or empty-release failure modes.
- **Validate on the tag again:** no race, but duplicates the full suite and was
  already rejected in ADR 0010.
- **Keep `release-gate` and add `always()` to the builds:** fixes the skip, but
  still races the tag against the main validation and still creates a published
  release before assets exist.
- **Auto-bump and release on every green `main`:** removes manual tags, but
  releases every merge and loses explicit control over the version and curated
  changelog.

## Follow-up

- [x] Move release builds into `release.yml` and reduce `build.yml` to
      validation.
- [x] Create the release as a draft and publish only after both APKs attach.
- [x] Update the release documentation and validation strategy.
- [ ] Link this ADR from the change summary.

# ADR 0012: Shell-mediated project file actions

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-30
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md#file-editing-and-worktrees), [state ownership](../architecture/state-and-data.md#project-file-browser), [issue 91](https://github.com/alvarolorentedev/opencode-mobile/issues/91)

## Context

V2 exposes filesystem listing, reading and writing but no rename, copy or move
endpoint. The Projects browser needs these operations, including copying between
worktrees on the same server, without moving orchestration into presentation.

## Decision

Use the existing V2 server-shell transport with a fixed, path-quoted POSIX
program owned by `lib/opencode/`. New mutations are unavailable on V1 and on
servers without the required shell utilities. Copy path remains device-local.

- `WorkspaceProvider` owns a process-local clipboard and mutation lock per
  connection; runtimes receive it through existing shared inputs. Disconnect,
  removal and settings changes clear that connection's clipboard.
- The browser's grouped actions own preflight, mutation and refresh orchestration.
  Swipe exposes Copy path, Rename and More; More and long-press use one actions
  sheet. Rename uses a focused sheet and Paste uses the browsed or selected folder.
- Validate project-relative paths and reject symlinks, special files, self-copy
  and nested destinations. Recursive sources containing symlinks are rejected.
- File replacement requires a destination fingerprint confirmed by the user and
  checked again before publication. Rename never replaces. Folder collisions
  never merge or replace, even after confirmation.
- Stage and verify copies before publication. Reserve new directory names with
  exclusive `mkdir`; a failed directory publication can leave a partial new copy,
  but never replaces an existing folder. Cut removes the source only after the
  published copy compares equal. Ambiguous results are reported without retries.

## Consequences

No dependency, compatibility adapter or persisted storage schema is added. File
operations have the existing shell time/output limits, so large directory copies
may fail. Shell commands cannot provide a transaction against concurrent external
filesystem edits. Errors retain the clipboard/input and distinguish uncertain or
partially completed moves from refresh failures. Both affected runtimes refresh
directory/search results, VCS status and active VCS diffs without changing focus.

Real-shell Vitest tests validate quoting, failure behavior and containment; the
V2 fake server models the positional program contract. Changed fake-server and
E2E contracts require human validation, plus real-server/device acceptance.

## Alternatives considered

- **Wait for upstream filesystem mutations:** cleaner contract, but blocks the
  requested feature. Revisit when native atomic operations exist.
- **Session shell commands or PTYs:** couple filesystem management to chats or
  interactive terminals rather than the existing scoped server-shell transport.
- **Directory overwrite or merge:** adds destructive ambiguity and rollback work
  unnecessary for the five core actions.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update owning implementation documentation and the ADR index.
- [x] Add real-shell, provider, fake-server and Projects flow coverage.
- [ ] Complete human and real-server/device acceptance before release.

# ADR 0013: Source-owned UI and complex forms

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-31
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: ADR 0006, ADR 0007
- Related: [Design system](../design/design-system.md), [Storybook](../design/storybook.md), [Component inventory](../design/component-inventory.md)

## Context

This agent-maintained application needs conventional source components and one
predictable styling system across native and web. Its full accent palettes,
workspace-scoped overlays, complex authentication forms and specialized
renderers must survive replacement of the previous UI foundation.

## Decision

Use React Native Reusables' Uniwind registry as the source-owned component
foundation, Uniwind Free with Tailwind CSS v4 for static styling, and RN
Primitives for standard accessible interactions. Remove React Native Paper.

- Author presentation values only in `constants/ui-tokens.json`. Generate CSS;
  derive TypeScript/native renderer values from the same source.
- Existing persisted preferences own light/dark/system and the six accents.
  Appearance synchronizes Uniwind's light/dark variable sets and navigation.
- Use conventional compound APIs, CVA variants and `cn()`. Keep measured,
  animated, keyboard and third-party renderer styles at their existing boundary.
- Complex forms use React Hook Form and Zod, reusing domain validators.
  Pin the Zod resolver adapter to 5.2.2: resolver 6's optional stable-Effect
  peer conflicts with the protocol dependency's pinned Effect prerelease.
  Form drafts remain local; API requests, persistence and domain state retain
  their existing owners. Simple preferences remain immediate.
- Keep one default portal host and named hosts inside native modal windows.
  Preserve workspace context, topmost dismissal, update blockers and focus.
- Preserve the native slider, terminal DOM interaction layer, markdown renderer
  and FlashList behavior. They implement specialized platform behavior.
- Storybook keeps its web/Vite role and renders production components with
  actual appearance and portal providers. Native acceptance still needs devices.
- Registry updates are reviewed source diffs with upstream provenance and
  local adaptations. Never overwrite the source catalog automatically.
- Superseded ADRs retain historical source paths; documentation tests still
  validate their Markdown links, structure and indexing, but do not require
  historical inline implementation paths to exist forever.

## Consequences

Agents can reuse ordinary source components and form conventions without a
Paper compatibility layer or parallel token values. The application owns
upstream adaptations and must review component upgrades. Native keyboard,
accessibility, modal stacking and production/FOSS builds remain acceptance
requirements; web tests cannot certify them.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep Paper:** retains the foundation the migration explicitly replaces.
- **A second styling engine or UI kit:** creates competing conventions.
- **Uniwind Pro:** unnecessary for the retained explicit animation and safe-area
  handling; the free engine supports the required Expo and Vite integration.
- **Generic form or overlay frameworks:** add indirection without another owner
  or consumer. Use focused local composition instead.
- **Replace the native slider with RN Primitives:** its native implementation
  does not provide drag handling, so replacement adds custom interaction code.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the design system and agent guidance.
- [x] Add generation checks and update reusable-component stories.
- [ ] Complete physical-device and signed distribution acceptance before release.

# ADR 0014: Scoped server data and explicit application lifecycles

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-31
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Provider ownership](0002-provider-centric-orchestration.md), [Realtime](0004-sse-with-polling-fallback.md), [State and data](../architecture/state-and-data.md)

## Context

Retained workspaces duplicate routine response storage and connection coordination.
Readiness polling also makes navigation depend on React publication timing.
Generic server caches and application workflows need separate owners.

## Decision

Use TanStack Query for routine server reads, with connection, authentication,
protocol and directory partitions. Retained/background workspaces remove their Query observers
(and held results) with empty query lists; query polling and automatic mutation replay stay disabled.
Existing domain contexts expose query-derived views without mirrored caches.

Use explicit React transitions for connection, workspace activation and Cloud
Link coordination. Resolve readiness from committed publications and propagate
cancellation through supported transports, retaining operation generations.
One connection owner supplies all retained projects. One shared SSE transport
continues to feed independent project-level reconciliation.

Keep sessions, transcripts, diffs, prompt admission, approvals, PTYs and voice
in their existing workflow owners. Native billing eligibility, purchases and
entitlement checkpoints remain outside routine query catalogs.

## Consequences

Server-data changes use ordinary typed queries and targeted invalidation.
Credential rotation replaces query partitions without remounting presentation
state. Capability snapshots retain their timestamps and cannot overwrite newer
network results. Existing persistence formats and protocol boundaries remain.

## Alternatives considered

- Keep bespoke caches: preserves duplicated request and freshness coordination.
- Put every workflow in Query: obscures streaming, uncertain writes and native checkpoints.
- Add XState: adds actor integration without removing the native transaction boundaries.
- Add Redux or Zustand: introduces another shared state owner.

## Rollback

Revert the migration and query-foundation commits together. Query data is
memory-only and persisted DTO versions remain unchanged; retain secure
credentials and preferences. No new native module or native build is required.

## Follow-up

Keep native purchase/entitlement and device lifecycle validation in the existing
manual workflow. Changes to browser/fake-server contracts retain the explicit
maintainer validation required by the repository agent instructions.

# ADR 0015: Feature-oriented implementation with shared runtime ownership

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-31
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: ADR 0002, ADR 0005
- Related: [Feature boundaries](../architecture/feature-boundaries.md), [Server data](0014-server-data-and-explicit-lifecycles.md), [UI foundation](0013-source-owned-ui-and-complex-forms.md), [Documentation router](../README.md)

## Context

A product change currently spans technical directories containing unrelated domains.
Agents need local feature ownership without duplicating the multi-workspace runtime,
query data, shared session lifecycle or native device resources.

## Decision

Group domain implementation and its Vitest tests under `features/`. Keep Expo Router
entrypoints in `app/`, native modules in `modules/`, and infrastructure in `shared/`.
`runtime/` owns cross-feature state and lifecycle composition. It mounts the same
application, connection and retained connection/project owners as before. Settings
and Onboarding may compose public UI from other features; they do not own those
features' state.

Use bounded named consumer and headless APIs. Context entrypoints remain separate
leaves so scoped portals can restore the existing context objects without importing
root composition. Enforce declared acyclic feature dependencies and keep transport,
secret persistence and native side effects outside arbitrary presentation.

The existing scope-aware Portal, OverlaySheet, Select and AlertDialog controls, and
the existing catalog/confirmation blockers, may import only the exact symbols in
`runtime/ui.ts` allowed by the architecture test. This exception preserves portal
ancestry, context identity and update-blocking lifetimes. It adds no bridge context,
state owner or general permission for shared UI to depend on runtime.

Retain ADR 0014's query keys, ownership, observer demand and cancellation. Retain ADR
0013's source-owned components, token source, form libraries, native renderers,
portal behavior and accessibility. Only implementation locations change. Protocols,
persistence formats, native discovery, routes and supported platforms do not change.

## Consequences

Agents begin in a feature and consult documented shared interfaces. State and actions
remain mounted independently of screens. Tests move with their owner; central tests
verify that every suite still matches Vitest discovery and TypeScript checking.
Existing size and context limits and compatibility isolation continue across all new
source directories. Historical source paths in immutable ADRs are interpreted using
the coordinated migration inventory; current documentation must resolve directly.

## Alternatives considered

- Feature-local workspace runtimes: duplicates session, connection and device owners.
- Keep only technical directories: preserves the navigation cost for every feature.
- Forwarding modules or parallel implementation trees: leave competing conventions.
- A new state library or monorepo framework: unnecessary for ownership and import checks.
- A new UI context bridge: adds another contract to preserve behavior already supplied
  by the existing scope-aware controls.

## Rollback

Revert the coordinated migration PR. Data keys, serialized formats, native module
identifiers and protocol contracts are unchanged; no data conversion is needed.

## Follow-up

Keep the public export policy, scoped agent guidance and documentation router aligned
with implementation. Do not increase limits or add compatibility paths to resolve a
boundary failure.

# ADR 0016: Supported Expo native integrations

- Status: Superseded by ADR 0017
- Date: 2026-10-31
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [ADR 0013](0013-source-owned-ui-and-complex-forms.md), [ADR 0014](0014-server-data-and-explicit-lifecycles.md), [ADR 0015](0015-feature-oriented-implementation.md), [Native integrations](../engineering/integrations-and-operations.md)

## Context

Native maintenance should follow the supported Expo SDK without replacing working
capabilities with incomplete alternatives. SDK 58 supplies a verified Apple store
environment API, an optimized Android template and compatible agent tooling.

## Decision

Use Expo SDK 58's dependency mapping and the existing CNG/build workflow. Keep
unrelated dependencies locked. Product policy stays in features; device resources
and third-party SDK calls remain behind shared platform interfaces. Retain the
single runtime owners and existing source-owned UI, Query and form conventions.

Android store updates use `expo-in-app-updates` with explicit immediate mode only.
Never call its automatic-selection helper. Existing readiness, unsaved-work and
foreground blockers apply before native handoff and interrupted-update recovery.
Cancellation keeps its cooldown. The native library may open Play Store on errors;
suppress the attempted version before handoff so returning cannot cause a loop.
A narrow patch disables the flexible native listener and its eager manager
initialization; completing one still requires the JS safety-gated handoff.
iOS uses Expo Application's verified production environment, the existing validated
listing lookup and explicit external App Store navigation, never a StoreKit sheet.

Keep the custom Android activity service: periodic background tasks do not replace
its ongoing notification and Headless JS behavior. Keep the ANR mitigation directly
after MainActivity's superclass call. Expo's Activity listener is invoked inside
the superclass delegate path, so identical timing has not been established.

Apply general dependency fixes with version-pinned patch-package diffs. Keep FOSS
transformations flavor-specific and build their modified dependencies from source.
Remove patches only when stable compatible upstream code preserves every fix.
Prefer awaited file writes; synchronous crash recording is retained because the
fatal handler must record before delegating. Load optional models only on demand;
active-conversation prewarming retains its latency purpose.

Official Expo skills stay developer-installed. MCP is optional, development-only,
explicitly enabled and absent from normal CI. Local build/log/device tools remain
sufficient without an Expo account or new recurring service.

## Consequences

The custom store-update module is removed. Sharing, Sherpa and legacy-update safety fixes, the activity
service and narrowly justified build plugins remain. Updating the SDK requires the
full existing gate and signed native/device acceptance; no native E2E framework
or mandatory CI job is added. FOSS publication remains subject to its existing
licensing and reproducibility requirements.

## Alternatives considered

- Flexible updates: the maintained package auto-completes downloads, which can
  interrupt later unsaved work. Immediate Play UI makes that tradeoff explicit.
- Replacing Android widgets: preserving installed receiver identities and headless
  snapshots is not established by SDK 58's new widget renderer.
- Replacing the MainActivity edit with a lifecycle listener: callback order differs.
- Removing every patch or taking prereleases: loses required safety/JNI fixes.
- Migrating custom modules to experimental APIs or adding a state/UI framework:
  adds unrelated churn without removing an existing required responsibility.

## Rollback

Revert the coordinated dependency/adapter/configuration commits with the lockfile
and regenerate native projects. Existing credentials, models and preferences stay
valid. After publication, release a forward fix with higher build numbers.

## Follow-up

- [x] Complete the existing automated gate and Android release/FOSS builds (local debug signing only).
- [ ] Complete the iOS distribution archive and signing checks.
- [ ] Complete signed Play immediate-update and public App Store acceptance.
- [ ] Complete physical-device voice, keyboard, widget and notification acceptance.
- [ ] Obtain explicit human validation of the changed E2E update contract.

# ADR 0017: Native defaults and prebuilt engines

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-31
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: [ADR 0016](0016-supported-expo-native-integrations.md)
- Related: [Native integrations](../engineering/integrations-and-operations.md), [Library decisions](../engineering/library-extraction.md)

## Context

The final migration requirements prefer the updater's upstream behavior and
require prebuilt Llama engines. These refine the adapter/patch choices in ADR
0016. The SDK 58 baseline, ownership, CNG conventions, exact content-capture
mitigation timing, FOSS exclusions, optional agent tooling and existing validation
policy from that decision remain in force.

## Decision

Use unmodified `expo-in-app-updates` 0.13.0. Call `startUpdate(true)` explicitly;
never use its automatic-selection helper or request flexible updates. Retain the
app's unsaved-work, route and foreground gates, cancellation cooldown and cold
recovery. Distinguish attempted handoffs from confirmed cancellations. The native
library keeps its default lifecycle, completion listener and automatic Play Store
fallback; JS does not intercept those native behaviors. Validate migration from
