the former flexible flow on signed store installations before release.

iOS retains Expo Application's verified production eligibility, validated listing
lookup and intentional external App Store navigation. Do not call the updater's
iOS StoreKit presentation API.

Pin `llama.rn` exactly to 0.12.9 with matching upstream Android engine binaries and
iOS XCFramework. Never enable engine source builds or override a source-only
release's restriction using stale binaries. Normal JNI/ObjC binding compilation
is required. Backport only the upstream iOS bridge type fix needed by current RN
headers. Reject the checked 0.13 candidates through rc.9 because they force Android
engine source builds. Keep model loading lazy and preserve the existing pack/API.

## Consequences

The updater policy patch is removed. Three pinned patches remain: Sharing input
safety, Sherpa ABI/iOS keys, and the Llama iOS binding backport. Their removal
conditions live in the library inventory. A clean lockfile install and native
builds verify the selected artifacts; physical/store acceptance remains required.
No new native E2E framework, CI workflow or recurring service is introduced.

## Alternatives considered

- Keep a custom Android updater: rejected in favor of the requested upstream
  package behavior and smaller local native ownership.
- Patch the updater's listener/lifecycle: rejected in favor of upstream defaults.
- Adopt Llama 0.13 candidates or force their prebuilt path: violates the prebuilt
  requirement or risks an engine/binding ABI mismatch.
- Drop optional native features: violates the supported functionality requirement.

## Rollback

Revert the coordinated migration commits and lockfile, then regenerate native
projects. Retain model files, credentials and preferences. Published builds require
a higher-numbered forward release; see the existing production validation matrix.

## Follow-up

- [x] Complete automated gates and Android development/production/FOSS builds plus unsigned iOS Release compilation for the pinned prebuilt set.
- [ ] Complete signed Play/App Store, migration and physical-device acceptance.
- [ ] Obtain explicit human validation of the changed E2E contracts.

# ADR 0018: Tag-driven release pipeline with static artifact verification

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-31
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: ADR 0011
- Related: [`.github/workflows/ci.yml`](../../.github/workflows/ci.yml), [`.github/workflows/release.yml`](../../.github/workflows/release.yml), [`scripts/ci/verify-android-release.mjs`](../../scripts/ci/verify-android-release.mjs), [Development](../engineering/development.md), [Validation strategy](../engineering/validation/strategy.md), [ADR 0019](0019-arm64-only-android-releases.md)

## Context

The repository had five workflows, a `workflow_run` dependency on a green
`Build` run, exact-SHA GitHub API lookups, a custom changed-path classifier, and
a separate manual iOS release. A tag push could not be the release command
without racing the main validation, and iOS was not part of the tag release.
Android and FOSS jobs duplicated setup and signing work.

A release also compiled and published artifacts without proving that the
installed production application could start. The WorkManager/R8 startup crash
in 1.0.110 showed that compilation and web E2E alone are insufficient. At the
same time, the project does not need a self-hosted emulator or paid device farm:
static artifact verification plus Google Play internal testing and TestFlight provide
the required release checks at low cost.

## Decision

Use exactly two workflow files:

- `ci.yml` runs on pushes to `main` and pull requests. It runs static checks,
  Vitest and architecture checks, fake-server validation, Storybook, FOSS
  preparation, the E2E budget and critical Playwright smoke flows. It never
  accesses release signing secrets.
- `release.yml` runs automatically on a `v*` tag. It verifies the tag, version
  and build numbers; requires the tagged commit to belong to `main`; runs the
  full release validation once; builds Android Play, FOSS Android and signed iOS
  in parallel; statically verifies every artifact; uploads validated Android
  builds to Google Play internal testing and iOS builds to TestFlight; and publishes the
  GitHub Release only after all mandatory jobs succeed.

The release does not require a manual dispatch, approval or release command for
normal internal releases. `workflow_dispatch` exists only for recovery and
rerunning an existing tag. Nothing is automatically promoted to a production
store track.

Android and FOSS builds use one ARM64-only release configuration. The release
workflow never uses emulator ABIs, a self-hosted runner or a paid device-testing
service. Static verification covers signing, package identity, version, ABI,
native libraries, R8/ProGuard safety, the WorkManager constructor, FOSS
exclusions and 16 KB page-size alignment. Static verification cannot prove
successful device startup; Google Play internal testing and TestFlight are the
real-device validation environments.

Release tags are protected against unauthorized creation, update and deletion.
Release secrets are available only to release jobs; only the GitHub publication
job has `contents: write`.

## Consequences

- Main and pull-request feedback is faster and predictable: static checks plus
  smoke, with no path classifier or gate job.
- Full browser E2E and native builds run once per release instead of on every
  main push.
- A tag push is sufficient to validate, build, distribute internally and publish
  a release. There is no exact-SHA polling or cross-workflow race.
- A failed validation, build or static artifact check blocks all distribution and
  GitHub publication.
- Google Play internal testing and TestFlight replace the proposed emulator gate for
  real-device startup validation. A device-only startup failure is found after
  internal distribution, not before it; the fix is a new version and tag.
- Release tags must never be moved. A failed release is fixed forward with a new
  version.
- The workflow files and their supporting scripts are the release authority; local
  full-gate and native-build commands are no longer mandatory before every push.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep `workflow_run` and exact-SHA validation:** rejected because it couples
  release to another workflow, races tag pushes and adds GitHub API coordination.
- **Run full E2E on every main push:** rejected because the tag release already
  runs the full suite and main feedback must stay fast.
- **Keep the manual iOS workflow:** rejected because it duplicates validation and
  signing and makes a tag release incomplete.
- **Add a hosted x86_64 emulator cold-launch job:** rejected because it requires
  emulator infrastructure and an extra production ABI. Static verification plus
  store internal testing is the chosen tradeoff.
- **Use a paid device-testing service:** rejected as unnecessary cost and
  operational complexity for this project.

## Follow-up

- [x] Replace the five workflows with `ci.yml` and `release.yml`.
- [x] Remove the changed-path classifier and exact-SHA validation lookup.
- [x] Add static Android release verification and ARM64-only artifacts.
- [x] Add Play internal and TestFlight distribution to the tag release.
- [x] Update AGENTS, development, validation and release documentation.
- [ ] Confirm the first tag release and record actual runtimes.

# ADR 0019: ARM64-only Android release artifacts

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-10-31
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [`scripts/build-android-release.mjs`](../../scripts/build-android-release.mjs), [`config/plugins/android.cjs`](../../config/plugins/android.cjs), [`scripts/ci/verify-android-release.mjs`](../../scripts/ci/verify-android-release.mjs), [`.github/workflows/release.yml`](../../.github/workflows/release.yml), [Integrations and operations](../engineering/integrations-and-operations.md), [ADR 0018](0018-tag-driven-release-pipeline.md)

## Context

Android release builds previously varied by trigger: tagged builds included
`armeabi-v7a` and `arm64-v8a`, while untagged builds could include `x86_64` for
emulators. Maintaining multiple release ABI configurations increased native
compilation time, artifact size and verification surface. The project does not
need to support 32-bit-only Android devices, and release validation no longer
uses an emulator.

Modern Android releases must also remain compatible with 16 KB memory pages.
That requirement applies to native library ELF alignment and APK zip alignment,
not to a particular device architecture.

## Decision

Every Android release artifact uses exactly `arm64-v8a`:

- Google Play APK and AAB
- FOSS/F-Droid APK
- Any local release build produced by `scripts/build-android-release.mjs`

`armeabi-v7a`, `x86` and `x86_64` are removed from release configurations. There
is no `ANDROID_RELEASE_ABIS` override, no per-tag ABI branch and no
emulator-specific release ABI. The Expo config plugin writes
`reactNativeArchitectures=arm64-v8a` into the generated release
`android/gradle.properties`; the release build script asserts the property and
also passes `-PreactNativeArchitectures=arm64-v8a`.

Release verification requires:

- only ARM64 native libraries in the APK and in the AAB base module;
- expected critical native libraries;
- 16 KB ELF `PT_LOAD` alignment for every native library;
- 16 KB APK zip alignment (`zipalign -c -P 16`);
- signing, package identity, version, R8/ProGuard and FOSS-exclusion checks.

Development builds are not release artifacts and may retain the Expo template
ABIs for local emulator use. No CI or release job builds or publishes them.

No emulator, self-hosted runner or paid device-testing service is added. Google
Google Play internal testing and TestFlight are the primary real-device validation
environments. Static artifact verification cannot guarantee successful device
startup.

## Consequences

- Android release builds are smaller and faster because only one native ABI is
  compiled and packaged.
- 32-bit-only Android devices are no longer supported. This is an intentional
  product decision, not a compatibility gap to revisit based on device reach.
- Prebuilt native libraries must remain 16 KB page-size compatible. A library
  that fails alignment blocks the release; it must be updated, patched or
  removed rather than shipped.
- Release verification is deterministic and does not depend on emulator
  availability or runner virtualization.
- Device-only startup, rendering or native initialization failures are found in
  Google Play internal testing or TestFlight. The fix is a new version and tag; release
  tags are never moved.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep `armeabi-v7a` for 32-bit devices:** rejected because it adds native
  build time and artifact size for a legacy audience the product does not need to
  support.
- **Keep `x86_64` for emulator acceptance:** rejected because the project does
  not add emulator infrastructure or a second production ABI for release checks.
- **Use a self-hosted emulator or paid device farm:** rejected as unnecessary
  operational cost; store internal testing is the real-device environment.
- **Ship without 16 KB verification:** rejected because modern Android and Play
  require 16 KB compatibility and the check is cheap and deterministic.

## Follow-up

- [x] Hardcode ARM64-only release ABI in the config plugin and build script.
- [x] Remove ABI overrides from CI and release workflows.
- [x] Add APK/AAB ABI, native-library and 16 KB alignment checks.
- [x] Update development, validation and F-Droid documentation.
- [ ] Confirm the first ARM64-only release artifact in Google Play internal testing.

# ADR 0020: Local-first observability with opt-in OTLP export

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-01
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [observability](../architecture/observability.md), [network resilience](../architecture/network-resilience.md), [F-Droid](../engineering/fdroid.md), [known gaps](../engineering/known-gaps.md)

## Context

The app already had a small request ring buffer, a per-day data-usage counter,
a synchronous last-JS-error file and a Diagnostics settings section. It had no
structured logging, persistent traces, metric aggregation, diagnostic export or
remote reporting. The existing error-reporting gap explicitly deferred remote
crash reporting because consent, scrubbing and a funded pipeline were missing.

The app runs on Expo SDK 58 / React Native 0.88 / Hermes and ships a FOSS variant
that must remain free of proprietary native libraries. Diagnostics must work
offline, must not collect prompts, source code, terminal output or credentials,
and must never make remote failures affect the product. Remote telemetry must be
independently controllable and must not transmit previously recorded local data.

## Decision

Use the OpenTelemetry JS SDK for tracing, metrics, logs, sampling, batching and
OTLP/HTTP export. Use `fflate` for ZIP/gzip. Keep only the local JSONL adapters,
sanitization, consent, local retention and the export manifest in
`shared/observability/`.

Local recording is enabled by default and bounded to approximately 7 days and
10 MB. Remote export is a generic OTLP/HTTP exporter, initially configured
for Grafana Cloud. It is disabled without credentials and in FOSS builds. The
master remote switch plus crash-report and performance categories live with the
existing global preferences; defaults are enabled for configured builds. The
exporter consumes only live events, has a memory-only bounded queue and is
stopped and cleared immediately when consent is revoked.

No native telemetry SDK is included. Native hard crashes/ANRs and remote stack
symbolication are therefore out of scope for this decision; local crash records
remain available and are ingested once into the local stream on the next launch.

## Consequences

- Local diagnostics work offline, in FOSS builds and without an account.
- Span/metric aggregation, OTLP serialization and retry behavior are maintained
  by the OpenTelemetry SDK instead of app code.
- Features expose only an allowlisted structured metadata surface; sanitization
  happens before persistence and again during export.
- Grafana Cloud (or any OTLP backend) can be enabled through build-time
  environment values without a backend server or native dependency.
- A bundled write token is extractable. It must be write-only, least-privilege
  and rotated; no read scopes. A build without credentials remains fully
  functional.
- Remote stack traces may be minified. Detailed local exports are the supported
  diagnostic attachment for issues.
- Adding a native crash adapter later must prove consent-safe initialization and
  FOSS exclusion before it is enabled.

## Alternatives considered

- **Winston:** rejected because it depends on Node streams/polyfills and is not
  a React Native runtime.
- **`react-native-logs`:** considered for the logging layer, but it only covers
  logs and would leave tracing, metric aggregation and OTLP as custom code. The
  OpenTelemetry SDK now covers all signals.
- **`loglayer`:** rejected because its transport ecosystem is Node/browser-first
  and adds packages without providing an Expo filesystem transport.
- **`expo-observe`:** rejected because it auto-collects and dispatches EAS
  Observe startup metrics in release builds by default, which conflicts with
  consent-first, local-first behavior.
- **`@grafana/faro-react-native`:** rejected because it adds
  `react-native-device-info`/MMKV and targets a Faro collector rather than a
  provider-neutral OTLP boundary.
- **`@sentry/react-native`:** deferred because native initialization and FOSS
  exclusion make consent revocation harder to guarantee. The exporter interface
  leaves room for a future isolated adapter.
- **A backend proxy:** rejected because diagnostics must work without Cloudflare
  or a hosted server, and a proxy would add an operational dependency.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update architecture, F-Droid, settings and functional-spec docs.
- [x] Add local, consent, export and OTLP tests.
- [x] Read Grafana Cloud connection values from release GitHub variables/secrets
  only for Android/iOS builds; FOSS and E2E builds never receive the token.
- [ ] Add a consent-safe native crash adapter only if a real device validation
  plan and FOSS exclusion proof exist.
- [ ] Revisit remote symbolication and retention cost after the first production
  telemetry window.

# ADR 0021: Per-connection custom CA trust

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-01
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [network resilience](../architecture/network-resilience.md), [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md), [known gaps](../engineering/known-gaps.md), [issue #92](https://github.com/alvarolorentedev/opencode-mobile/issues/92)

## Context

Self-hosted OpenCode servers often use a private CA (FreeIPA, step-ca, AD CS)
or a self-signed certificate. Android trusts only system CAs for apps targeting
API 24+, so the connection wizard fails before the user can reach the server.
The issue proposed trusting all user-installed CAs through Android's Network
Security Configuration. That would broaden trust for every host and every
connection, which is not acceptable for an app carrying source code and
developer credentials.

OpenCode 2 is the current contract. OpenCode 1 compatibility remains supported
for existing behavior, but this feature is not added to it: V1 connections keep
their existing system-trust behavior.

## Decision

Allow a user to import a certificate for one manual connection and trust it only
for that connection's `host:port`.

- System trust is always tried first; imported certificates are additive.
- Hostname verification, chain validation and expiry remain mandatory.
- CA, self-signed and non-CA leaf certificates are accepted. Non-CA anchors are
  labelled as pinned server certificates and require re-import on renewal.
- Cloud Link is excluded. Cloudflare terminates its TLS and the connection
  screen never offers the certificate control for Cloud Link profiles.
- V1 connections are excluded from the feature; the certificate is cleared when
  the setup probe detects OpenCode 1.
- Android installs a host-aware `SSLSocketFactory` and
  `X509ExtendedTrustManager` through the existing OkHttp custom-builder and
  factory hooks.
- iOS installs a host-scoped `NSURLProtocol` through the RN and Expo URLSession
  configuration providers, and a host-scoped `SRSecurityPolicy` through
  `RCTSetCustomSRWebSocketProvider`.
- The certificate is stored with AES-256-GCM using `expo-crypto`. The key lives
  in SecureStore and the ciphertext in AsyncStorage. The profile id is GCM
  additional authenticated data.
- `fetchConnection` registers saved trust before each request. Setup probes use
  temporary trust so an unsaved draft is only trusted during the probe.
- A certificate failure is a distinct, non-retryable connection failure kind and
  has actionable copy.

## Consequences

- Private-CA and self-signed V2 servers work on Android and iOS without trusting
  every user CA.
- Other connections, Cloud Link, update checks and unrelated hosts keep normal
  trust.
- The native module is a documented missing capability; it owns device trust
  only. Product policy and storage stay in `features/connections` and `shared/`.
- Certificate rotation for self-signed/non-CA anchors requires re-import.
- `expo-file-system` downloads bypass the custom trust in v1; API, SSE,
  attachments via `expo/fetch`, and WebSockets are covered.
- Revocation/OCSP is not checked.
- Native trust behavior requires device/simulator validation; CI cannot prove it.

## Alternatives considered

- **Global Android Network Security Configuration trusting user CAs:** simplest,
  but expands trust for every host and every connection. Rejected.
- **Certificate pinning packages:** pinning does not add a CA trust anchor and
  does not cover the SDK's SSE and RN WebSocket transports.
- **`react-native-blob-util` custom CA:** closest existing implementation, but
  its certificates are build-time resources and only its own fetch is covered.
- **Patch Expo/RN fetch:** version-fragile and still leaves WebSocket trust
  uncovered.
- **iOS system trust only:** works when the user installs a trusted profile, but
  does not provide connection-scoped inspection and removal.

## Follow-up

- [x] Add the shared certificate contract and encrypted store.
- [x] Add the Android and iOS trust modules.
- [x] Add probe status, error taxonomy and connection-screen controls.
- [x] Preserve V1 system-trust behavior and exclude Cloud Link.
- [ ] Validate on physical Android and iOS devices with a private CA and a
      self-signed certificate.

# ADR 0022: Markdown-first agent and command definitions with JSONC compatibility

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-01
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md), [Extensions feature](../../features/extensions/AGENTS.md)

## Context

OpenCode V2 loads agents from `{agent,agents}/**/*.md` and commands from
`{command,commands}/**/*.md`, in addition to the `agents` and `commands` keys in
`opencode.json(c)`. Markdown is the native authoring format for models,
permissions, prompts, and templates, but existing installations already contain
JSONC definitions.

The mobile Extensions surface previously managed commands only through JSONC and
treated file-backed commands as read-only. Adding agents there without changing
the format policy would either keep Markdown users locked out or migrate JSONC
files silently. Automatic migration is unsafe because Markdown directory entries
load after config documents and would override existing definitions.

The V2 API exposes `agent.list` and `command.list`, but neither returns a file
path or command body. File discovery and safe mutation therefore have to happen
through the server filesystem, with the API used as the reload authority.

## Decision

New agent and command definitions default to Markdown in the selected scope:

- project: `.opencode/agents/*.md` and `.opencode/commands/*.md`
- general: `<global config>/agents/*.md` and `<global config>/commands/*.md`

The app also discovers the official `agent` and `command` aliases, and the
legacy `mode`/`modes` agent directories. Markdown files are edited in place
until the user explicitly renames them. Legacy mode directories remain
read-only because the server forces those agents to `primary`.

Existing JSONC `agents` and `commands` definitions stay in JSONC and are edited
through the existing JSONC transaction. A new definition may explicitly choose
JSONC instead of the Markdown default. Nothing is migrated automatically.

When both a JSONC entry and a Markdown file define the same name in one scope,
Markdown is effective because the V2 loader processes the directory entry last.
The JSONC row remains visible as overridden, is not editable, and may be removed
without touching the Markdown file. Creating or renaming onto an existing name
is rejected across both formats and both scopes.

Markdown writes reuse the existing extension safety and transaction rules:
scope-owned paths, system/symlink/permission checks, a same-directory temporary
file, backup, atomic rename, exact-previous-content checking, read-back, server
reload polling, and rollback. Removed files move to `.opencode-mobile-trash`.
Frontmatter is parsed and edited with a real YAML parser; managed scalars and
permissions are validated locally, and generated objects are checked against the
installed OpenCode schema in tests.

## Consequences

- Users get one Extensions surface for both formats without losing existing
  definitions.
- The app depends on the server shell for file listing and mutation, matching
  the existing JSONC extension transaction. Windows and shell-less servers
  remain read-only for Markdown management.
- Command bodies are not exposed by the V2 API, so a body-only command edit can
  be confirmed only by exact file read-back and server name presence. Agent
  instructions can be confirmed through the effective `system` field.
- Duplicate definitions remain a server-side concern. The app detects and labels
  them, but does not choose a winner silently or delete the losing definition.
- Files retain a `.opencode-mobile.bak` backup beside edited Markdown. The
  existing scope-level backup restore UI continues to restore config backups;
  Markdown backups are used for automatic rollback.

## Alternatives considered

- **Convert JSONC definitions to Markdown:** rejected because it silently
  changes precedence and removes user-authored comments and advanced fields.
- **Markdown-only management:** rejected because JSONC is still an officially
  supported V2 configuration format.
- **Parallel extension configuration framework:** rejected because the feature
  already owns a scoped snapshot, serialized mutations, and transaction helpers;
  a second owner would duplicate query and state lifecycles.
- **Hand-written frontmatter parser:** rejected because YAML scalars, nested
  permissions, block values, and alias limits need a real parser to avoid
  corrupting files the server later rejects.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the API contract, functional specification, and component inventory.
- [x] Add Markdown codec, JSONC agent, snapshot, fake-server, and E2E coverage.
- [x] Link this ADR from the Extensions feature guidance.

# ADR 0023: Focused extension editors with structured authoring

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-01
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Settings components](../design/components/settings.md), [Functional specification](../product/functional-spec.md#extensions-section-v2), [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md#extensions-and-config-files), [ADR 0022](0022-markdown-first-extension-definitions.md)

## Context

Extension lists were preceded by inline creation forms and configuration paths.
Choosing an agent model required a provider/model string, local MCP setup
required a JSON argument array, and editing skills required the whole source.
The app already owns model catalogs, searchable pickers, scoped overlays and
safe definition mutations; another state owner or configuration format is not
needed.

## Decision

Show each extension inventory first and open focused editors in the existing
workspace-scoped overlay infrastructure. Agents, skills and commands separate
Setup from Instructions without saving or resetting when switching tabs.

- Agent model selection reuses the public AI picker, including inheritance,
  catalog search and variants. Custom IDs remain under Advanced. Editing an
  extension does not change chat model preferences.
- Local MCP setup collects an executable and separate literal arguments. It
  never parses a shell command. Remote setup collects an HTTP(S) URL.
- V2 permissions use ordered action/resource/effect rows. Legacy or custom
  shapes remain source-editable without implicit conversion.
- Skill structured edits retain unknown YAML fields and comments. Advanced
  source editing remains available. Existing IDs and storage formats stay
  stable unless an existing explicit rename operation is used.
- Dirty editor dismissal requires confirmation; failed writes retain the draft.
  Configuration paths and backup recovery live in a disclosure, while blocking
  safety warnings stay visible.

## Consequences

The common setup path no longer requires configuration syntax. Protocol codecs
remain responsible for serialization and preservation; feature forms forward
existing domain actions. Optional AI picker inputs retain existing chat behavior.
This supplements ADR 0022 and does not migrate definitions or change endpoints.
Preservation tests and existing extension/settings/chat flows cover the new UI;
native keyboard, Back and screen-reader behavior still need human acceptance.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep inline forms and replace only the model field:** leaves existing
  extensions below creation forms and preserves the other syntax-heavy inputs.
- **Convert all configuration to a new simplified schema:** risks losing custom
  fields, rule ordering and storage precedence.
- **A mandatory creation wizard:** adds steps to repeated edits. Tabs support
  direct access without making users finish an ordered sequence.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update implementation docs and component inventory.
- [x] Add protocol preservation tests and update existing E2E flows.
- [ ] Complete native keyboard, Back and accessibility acceptance.

# ADR 0024: Secure OpenID Connect authorization for connections

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-02
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [network resilience](../architecture/network-resilience.md), [state and data](../architecture/state-and-data.md), [library inventory](../engineering/library-extraction.md), [functional specification § Connection management](../product/functional-spec.md#connection-section), [feature boundaries](../architecture/feature-boundaries.md)

## Context

Manual connections authenticate with basic auth or gateway headers. Servers
behind an identity-aware proxy (Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, Authelia) often
expect a short-lived bearer JWT instead. Asking a mobile user to paste a token is
not viable: tokens expire, cannot be renewed, and end up in screenshots and
clipboard history.

The app already supports per-connection gateway headers in secure storage and a
per-connection custom CA. The connection screen and shared transport are the
natural owners for provider configuration and token use. The flow must protect
credentials across authorization, refresh and API requests, including outages,
redirects, sign-out and connection replacement.

The in-app WebView is not acceptable for sign-in: the app can read everything
typed into it. The token endpoint must never receive a client secret, because a
secret shipped on a phone is not a secret.

## Decision

Support the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE for public OpenID
Connect clients, per manual connection. Use maintained `expo-auth-session` for
PKCE, OAuth state and system-browser coordination; keep connection-specific
trust, persistence and session lifecycle rules in the app's existing owners.

- Configure issuer, client ID, scopes, token header and an optional callback
  override as non-secret profile metadata. Require a matching issuer in the
  discovery document. Issuer, authorization, token and token-bearing server
  endpoints require HTTPS, except explicit HTTP loopback development hosts.
- Use the registered `opencodemobile://oidc-callback` app callback, validate the
  exact callback target and OAuth state, and reject ambiguous response
  parameters. HTTPS app links and Expo Go callbacks are unsupported because
  they are not registered.
- Restrict API credentials to the configured secure origin and proxy mount.
  Reject redirects on discovery, token, API and OIDC terminal WebSocket
  requests, including in the iOS custom-CA fetch path. Only OIDC terminal
  sockets request redirect rejection; legacy sockets retain their policy.
- Store tokens with AES-256-GCM via `expo-crypto`; keep the key in SecureStore
  and ciphertext in AsyncStorage, keyed by connection scope, issuer and client
  ID. Refresh 60 seconds before expiry and coalesce requests by the access token
  actually rejected. Session generations and serialized storage operations
  prevent stale refresh/browser work from restoring credentials after sign-out,
  replacement or profile removal. Caller cancellation does not cancel another
  caller's shared refresh.
- Clear a session only for a definitive `invalid_grant` response on HTTP 400 or
  401. Preserve credentials for network, timeout, rate-limit, server,
  malformed-response and configuration failures. Never display untrusted
  provider error text and never open a browser without an explicit user action.
- Send the raw access token in the configured header, defaulting to
  `X-Auth-Request-Access-Token`. Preserve Basic `Authorization` and gateway
  headers; use `Authorization: Bearer` only when no password is configured.
  Retry once after 401/403 only when the request body is absent or a string.
- Android uses a pinned React Native source patch to reject redirects on OIDC
  WebSocket upgrades; iOS already rejects WebSocket redirect handshakes. Build
  React Native from source on Android so the patch ships.
- Affect only the manual V2 connection path. Do not add a V1 adapter; preserve
  Cloud Link, Basic, gateway-header, custom-CA and non-OIDC transport behavior.
  Load the OIDC stack on demand. Web sign-in reports an explicit unsupported
  error because the app cannot intercept its callback there.

## Consequences

- Users can connect to identity-aware servers without copying tokens, and a
  roaming device renews the session without re-opening the browser.
- The mobile app becomes a public OIDC client. Providers must register the
  registered callback and allow PKCE. Providers that require a client secret,
  DPoP, mTLS or another callback scheme are out of scope.
- Provider outages no longer sign users out, and stale work cannot resurrect a
  signed-out or replaced session.
- Android builds take longer while React Native is built from source to include
  the redirect policy patch. Installing the native socket change requires a
  native build; it cannot ship in an OTA JavaScript update.

## Alternatives considered

- **In-app WebView sign-in:** rejected; the app could read the user's password
  and the flow would look like phishing.
- **Paste a JWT manually:** rejected; no renewal, poor usability, and tokens leak
  into clipboard managers.
- **Client-secret (confidential) client:** rejected; a secret on a device is not
  a secret, and PKCE is the correct mechanism for public clients.
- **Hand-written PKCE and browser coordination:** rejected; maintained Expo
  AuthSession already provides these primitives, while app-owned rules still
  handle connection-specific trust and session state.
- **Replace the complete session manager with a library:** rejected; libraries
  do not own connection-scoped persistence or the app's lifecycle guards.
- **Disable all WebSocket redirects:** rejected; this changes non-OIDC
  connection behavior.
- **Trust returned provider descriptions:** rejected; they may disclose
  echoed credentials.
- **Automatic browser popup after a 401:** rejected; it interrupts unrelated
  work and is indistinguishable from an attack when it happens unprompted.
- **Store tokens in SecureStore values:** rejected; JWT plus refresh token
  routinely exceeds SecureStore's 2 KB value guidance on Android. The existing
  certificate store already establishes AES-GCM + SecureStore key as the
  pattern for larger secrets.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs and dependency inventory.
- [x] Add contract, transport, session and native regression coverage.
- [ ] Validate real-provider browser round trips and native redirects on devices.

# ADR 0025: Server-exposed plugin commands

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-03
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [issue 98](https://github.com/alvarolorentedev/opencode-mobile/issues/98), [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md#server-plugin-commands), [ADR 0003](0003-v2-first-protocol-boundary.md)

## Context

V2 plugins register commands in the server's effective location-scoped registry.
A cached-name check in Mobile can miss new registrations and send slash text as
an ordinary prompt. TUI commands also include actions with no server API.

## Decision

Use the existing server command catalog and session command operation for V2
plugin compatibility. Let the server resolve names/overrides and report unknown
commands; never turn a rejected command into a prompt. Revalidate catalogs on
demand/lifecycle transitions and authoritative events through existing Query
owners, without command polling or a second registry. Preserve V1 behavior.

## Consequences

Server-exposed commands and hooks work without executing plugin code on Mobile.
Autocomplete can briefly lag a server change, but execution is authoritative.
Compatibility excludes TUI/desktop UI and unavailable APIs. Real-server fixture
coverage complements deterministic UI and lifecycle tests.

## Alternatives considered

- **Mobile plugin runtime or hardcoded TUI parity:** duplicates server behavior
  and cannot represent UI-only handlers through the command API.
- **Continuous catalog polling:** unnecessary when update events and lifecycle
  revalidation already provide the relevant refresh points.

## Follow-up

- [x] Document the compatibility boundary and real-server validation.
- [x] Cover command routing, lifecycle refresh and a real V2 plugin.
- [x] Expose V2 `session.compact` and `session.generate` as the `/compact` and
  `/btw` built-ins. This is not general TUI parity: other TUI commands still
  need a server API before they can be listed or executed.

# ADR 0026: Metadata-driven agent selection

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-03
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md), [chat components](../design/components/chat.md), [OpenCode V2 selection](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/4617210822bdbb31e5749751afbfb4584ccedac8/packages/core/src/agent.ts)

## Context

Discarding agent mode and visibility exposed hidden maintenance agents and
subagent-only agents in the primary picker. Previously saved IDs also bypassed
picker behavior during prompt and command execution. Older V1 responses and
existing capability snapshots may omit metadata entirely.

## Decision

Keep the full server catalog, but require explicit `primary` or `all` mode and
`hidden !== true` for primary selection on both protocols. Never infer eligibility
from an agent's name or missing metadata. Preserve visible subagents for mentions;
hidden agents remain available to server-owned delegation. Disabled agents are
removed by the server before listing.

Resolve stored choices against this eligible catalog, then the configured
`default_agent`, Build, and server order. Preserve preferences if no eligible
replacement exists; block prompt/command submission until eligibility is known.
Recheck at execution independently of preference reconciliation.

## Consequences

Custom and plugin agents follow the same rules as built-ins. No new state owner,
V1 adapter, or persistence format is required. Old caches remain readable and
refresh normally, but cannot establish eligibility without mode metadata.
V1 servers omitting mode no longer permit primary selection or submission;
this explicit compatibility limitation avoids guessing whether an agent is safe
to select. Servers returning metadata retain their existing execution protocol.

## Alternatives considered

- **Name blacklist:** rejects legitimate overrides and cannot cover custom internal agents.
- **Treat missing mode as selectable:** preserves older behavior but cannot establish eligibility.
- **Filter the shared catalog:** removes subagents needed by mentions and delegation.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update protocol, persistence, and chat implementation docs.
- [x] Cover selectors, execution, hydration, and browser behavior.

# ADR 0027: Sandboxed mobile host for OpenCode GUI plugins

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-03
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [plugin GUIs](../architecture/plugin-guis.md), [feature boundaries](../architecture/feature-boundaries.md), [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md)

## Context

OpenCode V2 plugins may ship a `./gui-experimental` CommonJS bundle. OpenCode
Desktop evaluates that bundle in its renderer and gives it a broad `ctx` API.
The mobile app has no equivalent host: it has no desktop side region, session
tab strip, Electron main process, `WebContentsView` or native application menu.
The published `@opencode/plugin` package also does not export the host loader or
the Solid contexts that `usePlugin` and `usePanel` read.

Running third-party bundles in the app's React Native realm would expose the
server credential and the whole app state. That is not acceptable for npm code.

## Decision

Host plugin GUIs in the existing Expo DOM WebView surface, one plugin per view.
Evaluate the CommonJS bundle with a small local loader and a capability-scoped
`ctx` shim implemented in `features/extensions/ui/`:

- provide identity, options, app metadata, i18n, sessions, servers, RPC/session
  reads, panels, styles, dialogs, toasts, storage, layout, tabs and the small
  `ctx.ui` DOM kit;
- leave `ctx.main`/Ipc, `ctx.embeds`, `ctx.desktop`, native menus, contracts and
  native UI components unsupported or inactive;
- pass **no** server credential into the WebView; RPC and session reads go
  through a native bridge that uses the connection's authenticated client;
- scope RPC calls to the plugin id, allow only the current session for
  `session.get`, validate external URLs, and block direct network APIs in the
  WebView;
- render plugin styles into a Shadow DOM and mount the selected panel in a
  large chat overlay, defaulting to the first. Multiple panels get a host
  dropdown. This is the profile implemented at `MOBILE_GUI_API = 1`.

The bundle format is not changed. The host treats it as a public, unstable
input: unknown modules, a newer `api`, a missing export, or a setup failure
fails closed and leaves the host usable.

## Consequences

- Flowgraph, and other panel-first plugins, can render without app-specific
  branches.
- The host does not support the full desktop contract. Plugins using `ctx.main`,
  `ctx.embeds`, `ctx.desktop`, contracts or native `ctx.ui` are degraded or
  unsupported; the UI must say so.
- The WebView is a security boundary, not a process sandbox. Direct network is
  blocked best-effort; a future bridge inside a sandboxed iframe with CSP is the
  upgrade path.
- Plugin UI is DOM, not native. Accessibility, dynamic type and safe-area
  behavior need host chrome and device validation.
- The local loader and `ctx` shim must track the experimental upstream API and
  the `MOBILE_GUI_API` profile.

## Alternatives considered

- **Full desktop host shim:** rejected for now. It requires reimplementing the
  desktop side region, tabs, palette, settings, native UI kit and main process,
  and the published SDK does not expose the host contexts.
- **Run bundles in Hermes with a DOM shim:** rejected. Solid DOM, CSS and mermaid
  require a browser rendering engine.
- **Declarative mobile view model over RPC:** safer, but not compatible with
  existing `gui-experimental` plugins; retained as an opt-in future mode.
- **Embed the OpenCode web app in a WebView:** rejected as a mobile host. It is
  not native UX, and the web app does not load third-party GUI bundles.

## Follow-up

- [x] Add the generic loader, capability-scoped context and panel route.
- [x] Add flowgraph-compatible RPC/session/panel fixtures and loader tests.
- [ ] Add a manifest/API handshake upstream and broaden the supported surface.
- [ ] Move the plugin frame into a sandboxed iframe with an explicit CSP.
- [ ] Validate on iOS and Android devices.

# ADR 0028: Runtime RTL direction follows the interface language

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-04
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Localization integration](../engineering/integrations-and-operations.md#localization), [Design system](../design/design-system.md#accessibility-localization-and-feature-acceptance)

## Context

The persisted interface-language preference can differ from the device locale.
Native RTL detection based only on the device language therefore leaves the app
in the wrong layout direction when the user selects Arabic or Hebrew in app
settings. Expo Router also needs the selected direction for navigation gestures
and transitions.

## Decision

Derive layout and Expo Router direction from the resolved i18n language. Apply
that direction at the app root, modal surfaces, and shared selection and sheet
hosts. Set the web document's `lang` and `dir` attributes from the same resolved
language.

Keep terminal, code, diff, path, URL, and identifier content in its natural
left-to-right order within right-to-left interface copy.

## Consequences

Changing the in-app language updates layout direction with the existing
translation change. Native RTL support remains enabled in the Expo localization
config so system RTL languages are also supported. Shared controls and feature
surfaces must use logical layout and mirror directional navigation affordances.

## Alternatives considered

- **Use only the device locale:** it conflicts with the persisted in-app language
  preference and leaves manually selected RTL languages in LTR layout.
- **Force RTL globally through `I18nManager`:** it persists independently of the
  language choice and takes effect only after an app restart.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Extend the locale catalog and plural-category contract.
- [x] Link this ADR from the localization implementation doc.

# ADR 0029: Minimal remote telemetry budget

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-04
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [ADR 0020](0020-local-first-observability-and-otlp.md), [observability](../architecture/observability.md)

## Context

The broad instrumentation added with ADR 0020 emitted sampled spans, request and
latency metrics, and handled-error logs. That volume exhausted the Grafana Cloud
metrics and traces capacity, while most of the data duplicated local diagnostics
that are already available on-device.

Remote telemetry still needs a small product signal: how many servers use the V1
and V2 OpenCode protocols.

## Decision

Keep the local-first diagnostics pipeline, but limit remote export to:

- unhandled exceptions, fatal JavaScript errors, and unhandled rejections as OTLP
  logs under Crash reports;
- one counter, `server.contract`, with a bounded `v1`/`v2` label, recorded once
  per server per launch under Usage diagnostics.

Do not emit remote spans. Remove HTTP request traces and request/retry metrics.
Handled domain failures, including voice capture failures, stay in the local
JSONL store and are never uploaded. Adding a metric or span requires an explicit
product request and an update to the observability documentation.

## Consequences

- Grafana volume is bounded by crashes plus one low-cardinality counter.
- Connection, SSE, polling, transcript, notification and tool timings remain
  available locally through Recent activity and diagnostic exports.
- Performance regressions are no longer visible remotely; reproduce them from a
  local export when needed.
- The OpenTelemetry trace and metric SDKs stay in place so a future approved
  signal does not need a new backend integration.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep sampled traces and rely on retention:** rejected because sampling still
  exhausted the provisioned traces capacity.
- **Keep only error spans:** rejected because the same unhandled errors already
  arrive as crash logs, so error spans duplicated volume.
- **Drop the remote metric path entirely:** rejected because the V1/V2 server
  distribution is the one signal currently requested.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the observability and settings documentation.
- [x] Remove HTTP spans, request metrics, and handled-error uploads.
- [x] Add the bounded `server.contract` counter.
- [ ] Revisit this budget only when a new signal is explicitly requested.

# ADR 0030: Server-archived project visibility without a client archive write

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-04
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md#project-and-sessions), [Functional specification](../product/functional-spec.md#2-pick-a-project), [Projects feature](../../features/projects/AGENTS.md)

## Context

OpenCode archives a project automatically when its known directories have been
missing for an hour. The server marks it with `time.archived` and excludes it
from the default `project.list()` result. Resolving the directory through
`location.get` clears the marker.

The V2 protocol has no endpoint that archives or deletes a project on demand.
`project.update` accepts canonical, name, icon, and commands only. The desktop
web UI's "Other projects" section is not a server archive; it is the local set
of server projects this client has not opened, and its Close action only removes
a project ID from that local set.

The pinned `@opencode/client` 2.0.16 cannot request archived projects or read
`time.archived`. Version 2.2.5 exposes `project.list({ archived: true })` and the
archived timestamp.

## Decision

Upgrade the V2 client to 2.2.5 and expose server-archived projects as a
read-only, on-demand catalog behind a picker toggle.

- The normal project list stays on the server's default `project.list()`, which
  already excludes archived projects.
- The archived list is fetched with `project.list({ archived: true })`, filtered
  to entries with `time.archived`, and never persisted.
- Restore calls `location.get` for the archived directory. It works only when
  the directory exists again; failure keeps the row and reports the server
  reason.
- The app does not add a user-triggered archive action. The existing close action
  remains local to the device and does not touch the server.
- The archived list is V2-only. V1 connections hide the toggle.

## Consequences

Users can discover and restore projects the server archived, instead of having
to remember and retype the directory. The normal list keeps its existing
semantics and cache invalidation, and the archived query shares the `projects`
event resource so `project.updated` refreshes both.

The client upgrade is a generated-protocol change: the dependency, mappers,
contract tests, fake server, and full E2E gate must be updated together. Older
V2 servers that reject the `archived` query degrade to an unavailable archived
section without affecting the normal list.

## Alternatives considered

- **Local archive only:** rejected because it cannot show or restore projects
  the server already archived, and it remains device-scoped.
- **Add an archive action to `project.update`:** rejected because the server
  type has no archived field and the app must not invent an unsupported write.
- **Delete or move the project directory to trigger the sweep:** rejected as
  destructive and outside the app's authority.
- **Keep the pinned 2.0.16 client:** rejected because archived projects cannot be
  read at all; the user chose the upgrade.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Add fake-server coverage for archived listing and restore.
- [x] Link this ADR from the change summary.

# ADR 0031: Flexible store updates with explicit install

- Status: Superseded by ADR 0036
- Date: 2026-11-05
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: [ADR 0017](0017-native-defaults-and-prebuilt-engines.md)
- Related: [App updates](../product/app-updates.md), [Library decisions](../engineering/library-extraction.md), `patches/expo-in-app-updates+0.13.0.patch`

## Context

Immediate-only updates interrupt the user with a blocking Play flow at download
time. Play's flexible mode downloads in the background while the app stays
usable, but `expo-in-app-updates` 0.13.0 installs the moment a flexible download
finishes (`completeUpdate()` inside the `DOWNLOADED` listener), so the app
cannot gate the restart behind its unsaved-work, route and foreground blockers.
ADR 0017 therefore standardized on unmodified upstream behavior with explicit
immediate requests only.

## Decision

Patch `expo-in-app-updates` 0.13.0 with `patch-package` and keep everything else
upstream. The patch stops the automatic install on download completion, reports
a finished download from `checkForUpdate`, and reports the store version for an
interrupted immediate update so recovery keeps the offered version. The adapter
(`shared/platform/android-app-updates.ts`) prefers immediate and falls back to
flexible when Play only permits that type. A finished download surfaces a
Restart & install banner; the install runs only after an explicit tap
re-verifies safety. JS never auto-installs. The `llama.rn` pinning, FOSS
exclusions, SDK baseline and remaining ownership from ADR 0017 stay in force.

## Consequences

Flexible downloads no longer restart the app during unsafe work, and updates
remain offerable where Play disallows immediate mode. The patch is owned
locally: every `expo-in-app-updates` upgrade must re-verify it, and signed
Play internal-track acceptance must cover download, kill-during-download,
busy-at-completion and install. Flexible mode lets users defer the install
indefinitely; availability-gated protocol changes must account for stale
clients. iOS keeps explicit App Store navigation.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep immediate-only:** rejected; it blocks the user at download time and
  suppresses offers where Play only permits flexible updates.
- **Auto-install on download completion:** rejected; the restart would bypass
  the app-side safety gates this change exists to protect.
- **Custom Android updater:** rejected in favor of the maintained bridge with
  one narrow patch.
- **Upstream contribution:** accepted as follow-up; drop the patch if upstream
  makes auto-complete optional.

## Follow-up

- [ ] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [ ] Add or update tests or fake-server coverage.
- [ ] Link this ADR from the change summary.

# ADR 0032: Project picker matches web Used/Other semantics

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-05
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [ADR 0030](0030-server-archived-projects.md), [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md#project-and-sessions), [Functional specification](../product/functional-spec.md#2-pick-a-project), [Projects feature](../../features/projects/AGENTS.md)

## Context

The mobile picker built its list as the union of the locally opened projects and
the server catalog, so stale local opens (deleted folders, old temp dirs,
pre-upgrade entries) rendered as full rows. On a real server the phone showed
many more projects than the web client, whose settings list renders only the
server catalog split into used and a collapsed Other projects section.

## Decision

The picker renders the server catalog only, split per connection into Used
(opened on this device + connection, matched by root path or any known checkout
directory) and a collapsed Other projects section with its count, exactly like
the web client. Searching expands Other and filters every section.

Locally opened folders the server no longer reports never become rows. They are
listed in a collapsed "Unavailable on this server" section with remove actions
only, so selecting them cannot mount a runtime for a dead folder. Retained
runtimes whose root left the server catalog are likewise dropped from the rows
(while no runtime on the connection reports a catalog, active roots are kept so
a cold start never flashes empty). `buildOpencodeProjects` now maps the server
catalog in server order; the opened list only marks usage.

## Consequences

Phone and web show the same project set. Stale entries are cleanable instead of
confusing, and closing a project still only removes the local entry. The picker
query key and invalidation are unchanged; the archived-projects view is
unchanged.

Existing E2E expectations that asserted an unopened server project is visible
without expanding Other were updated to expand the section first.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the union and badge stale rows inline:** rejected because the main list
  stays inflated and diverges from the web client.
- **Auto-delete stale opens on catalog load:** rejected because a worktree
  inventory that has not loaded yet could make a live checkout look stale;
  hiding with an explicit remove action is safer.
- **Probe stale paths with `location.get` to revalidate:** rejected because
  resolving persists a project on the server as a side effect.

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Add picker-split unit tests and update the affected E2E specs.

# ADR 0033: Server-driven projects and sessions without local registries

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-05
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: [ADR 0032](0032-web-parity-project-picker.md)
- Related: [API contract](../architecture/api-contract.md#project-and-sessions), [Functional specification](../product/functional-spec.md#2-pick-a-project), [State and data](../architecture/state-and-data.md#project-and-session-identity-state)

## Context

ADR 0032 split the picker into Used and Other backed by a locally persisted opened-project list. That list is a second source of truth: any directory the app ever recorded renders as long as the local store says so, which is exactly how the phone showed projects (`/home/alvarolorentedev`, deleted folders, old temp dirs) the web client never listed. Patching the symptoms (hiding stale rows, an Unavailable cleanup section) keeps the registry and its drift.

## Decision

Project and chat identity comes from the server catalogs only. The app deletes its project registries and keeps just one local exception.

- Delete the opened-project list (`opencode-mobile.projects`, `projects-storage.ts`, the `openProject`/write-back paths, `closeProjects`, and `projectClosedValues`), the active-project pointer, and the last-session map (`opencode-mobile.last-session-by-project`, `last-session-storage.ts`). Stored values from older builds are removed once on hydrate.
- The picker renders the flat server catalog in server order. Selecting only changes the active selection; there is no close action and no Unavailable section because nothing local can go stale.
- On connect the retained placeholder runtime derives the active project from the server: the server default location first, then the most recently active project (`time_active` is bumped by location boots and durable session events, so it tracks real usage). An explicit target the server still resolves (deep link, worktree) is kept.
- Opening a project without an explicit selection picks the newest session in the server `session.list` (which defaults to newest-first). The bootstrap and reconcile fallbacks that preferred a remembered session now use `sessions[0]`.
- Connections still mount one placeholder runtime each and create project runtimes on demand via `ensure()`; composer drafts are safe because they live in presentation state, not in runtimes. Nothing about mounted projects is persisted, so a restart always re-derives from the server.
- Favorites stay as the single local exception: the server has no favorite flag.

## Consequences

The phone can never show a project or chat the server does not report, and all devices converge on the server-most-recent project at cold start. The cost is the loss of per-device last-open restore: reopening the app after working elsewhere opens the server-most-recent project instead of the one this phone last showed. Session transcript, session-list, and capability caches stay as transparent server-confirmed caches.

## Alternatives considered

- **Auto-prune stale opens once inventories settle:** rejected as a half measure; the registry and its write paths remain, along with the race between inventory loads and pruning.
- **Keep the active-project pointer as one persisted string:** rejected per the server-most-recent decision; the pointer is exactly the local truth this ADR removes.
- **Drop favorites too:** rejected; there is no server field to replace them with, and they are explicit user marks rather than derived identity.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Update unit, persistence, and E2E coverage for the removed registries.
- [x] Link this ADR from the change summary.

# ADR 0034: Device-local project archive marker

- Status: Superseded by ADR 0038
- Date: 2026-11-05
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [ADR 0033](0033-server-driven-projects-and-sessions.md), [ADR 0030](0030-server-archived-projects.md), [State and data](../architecture/state-and-data.md#project-and-session-identity-state), [Functional specification](../product/functional-spec.md#2-pick-a-project)

## Context

Projects are derived from the server catalog (ADR 0033): the device keeps no
opened-project list, active-project pointer, or last-session map. Users still
want to remove a server project from their own picker without changing the
server, as they can favorite a chat without a server flag. The server has no
project archive write; `project.update` has no archived field. Server-archived
projects remain a separate read-only catalog.

## Decision

Add one device preference that complements [ADR 0033](0033-server-driven-projects-and-sessions.md)
rather than superseding it: a hidden-project map keyed by connection scope. The
server catalog remains the only source of project rows.

- Persist `opencode-mobile.hidden-projects` as a connection scope to project
  path list. Validate it with a zod boundary, trim, dedupe, and cap each list at
  50 entries. Favorites remain the other local preference.
- The picker intersects the server catalog with the hidden set. A hidden path
  that the server no longer reports renders nothing and is inert; it never
  creates a row or hides a different project. No pruning is required.
- Main rows expose "Archive on this device". Hidden server projects move to a
  collapsed "Archived on this device (N)" section with Restore. Search expands
  and filters that section.
- The server-archived section keeps its separate "Archived on OpenCode" label
  and `project.list({ archived: true })` read. A project can carry both markers;
  because the normal catalog excludes server-archived projects, the server
  archived section wins until it is restored.
- Hiding the active project activates the first remaining visible server
  project on that connection. If none remains, the selection stays; the next
  picker open still uses the server-derived default. No active pointer is
  persisted and there is no clear-focus API.
- Connection-scope refreshes migrate the hidden markers with the same scope
  migration used for favorites.

## Consequences

Users can declutter a device without changing server state or showing rows the
server does not report. The hidden set is device-local and does not sync. A
hidden marker that outlives its project is harmless; it simply matches nothing.
The cost is one more persisted preference and a second archived-style section
that must stay visibly distinct from the server-archived section.

## Alternatives considered

- **Rekey project identity to a server project ID:** rejected because stored IDs
  could later hide a different project; paths match the rendered catalog
  directly, and stale paths are inert.
- **Add or emulate a server archive write:** rejected; the server exposes no
  archive field and the app must not edit canonical directories or invent an
  unsupported mutation.
- **Restore the opened-project registry:** rejected; it is the second source of
  truth ADR 0033 removed. This marker only subtracts from the server catalog.
- **Persist the active project when the hidden row was active:** rejected;
  activation uses the remaining server catalog and the next cold start keeps
  deriving from the server.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Add storage, split-helper, persistence, and picker flow coverage.
- [x] Link this ADR from the change summary.

# ADR 0035: Live token highlighting in the composer

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-05
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Chat components](../design/components/chat.md), [composer accent rules](../../features/chat/model/composer-accent.ts), [composer input](../../features/chat/ui/chat-prompt-input.tsx), [transcript markdown](../../features/chat/ui/chat-markdown.tsx), [ADR 0017](0017-native-defaults-and-prebuilt-engines.md)

## Context

The composer must visually distinguish `@` references, agents, and skills from
leading `/` commands while the user types. React Native's `TextInput` cannot
style substrings, so a plain input can only render one text color. The transcript
already renders through `react-native-enriched-markdown`, which exposes per-link
variants; the composer has no equivalent hook.

A custom overlay (a styled `Text` behind a transparent input with synchronized
scroll) would add selection, caret, wrapping, and scroll-alignment risk on every
platform. The alternative is a maintained native input that owns that behavior.

## Decision

Use `@expensify/react-native-live-markdown` pinned to `0.1.371` for the native
prompt input. The package supports the New Architecture and RN 0.88, and its
custom parser runs as a worklet on the UI thread. `features/chat/ui/chat-prompt-input.tsx`
renders it on iOS and Android and keeps the shared `Input` on web, where the
live highlight is not offered.

The parser in `features/chat/model/composer-accent.ts` emits overlapping `bold`
and `mention-user`/`mention-here` ranges. The package's mention styles only expose
color and background, so the separate bold range is what makes tokens bold in the
theme tint. The input value remains plain text; no prompt or markdown semantics
change.

Import the package's built `MarkdownTextInput` module directly. The package entry
also re-exports its default ExpensiMark parser, which pulls `expensify-common`
and requires a workletized `html-entities`. The app does not use that parser.

Transcript text uses the same token rules. `chat-markdown.tsx` wraps surviving
tokens as `mention:`/`command:` links and styles them through `linkVariants`.
Code spans, fenced blocks, and existing links are masked first and never wrapped.
User bubbles use the dark palette tint because they stay dark in both themes;
flat and assistant bubbles use the active tint.

## Consequences

- The native app gains a native dependency and must be rebuilt. Device validation
  covers typing, IME, paste, selection, the iOS height cap, text scaling, RTL, and
  light/dark/accent themes. The tag release remains the authoritative native build.
- The deep import is deliberate. Keep it pointed at the built module and revisit it
  when the package gains a stable input-only entrypoint.
- The worklet parser skips drafts above 4,000 characters to keep the UI-thread
  scan cheap. Transcript masking uses simple regexes; nested or unclosed Markdown
  code/link constructs are a known limit.
- Web keeps the plain composer, so the accent is native-only there. The transcript
  accent works on all platforms.
- Tokens in bubbles are rendered as links for styling. `onLinkPress` ignores the
  custom schemes, and copy/TTS still use the raw transcript text.
- Dependency review follows ADR 0017: exact version, SDK-compatible package,
  FOSS/license check, and native rebuild.
- `patches/@expensify+react-native-live-markdown+0.1.371.patch` adapts the
  package's Android `latest` mounting patch to RN 0.88: `TextLayoutManager.measureText`
  now takes the `Context`, which 0.1.371 does not pass, so a clean Android build
  failed to compile. Drop the patch when a published release supports RN 0.88;
  `tests/vitest/live-markdown-patch.test.ts` guards the installed source.

## Alternatives considered

- **Overlay mirror:** no new dependency and full control, but duplicated text
  layout, caret/selection painting, and scroll synchronization are fragile across
  iOS, Android, and web.
- **`react-native-enriched-markdown` input:** already installed and supports bold
  link variants, but it is native-only and outputs Markdown, which would change
  draft semantics and leave web without an equivalent.
- **WebView rich editor:** heavy runtime, poor input latency, and a large
  accessibility and security surface for a single-line-style prompt.
- **Plain input with no accent:** smallest change, but does not satisfy the
  requested composer affordance.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the chat and functional-spec documentation.
- [x] Add parser and markdown-style Vitest coverage.
- [ ] Complete native device validation and the release build.
- [ ] Link this ADR from the change summary.

# ADR 0036: Flexible-first store updates with a Play urgency override

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-05
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: [ADR 0031](0031-flexible-updates-with-explicit-install.md)
- Related: [App updates](../product/app-updates.md), [Library decisions](../engineering/library-extraction.md)

## Context

ADR 0031 added flexible downloads with an explicit install, but ordered the
adapter immediate-first. Because Play normally permits immediate updates, the
blocking flow stayed the default and the background download was effectively
unreachable. The overlay UX only appears when flexible is requested first.

## Decision

Request flexible first in `shared/platform/android-app-updates.ts`; fall back to
immediate only when Play refuses flexible, and keep immediate for Play update
priorities 4-5, which the console uses to mark an urgent release. The patch,
deferred install behind the safety gates, cooldowns, recovery and every other
clause of ADR 0031 remain in force unchanged.

## Consequences

Ordinary releases download in the background while the app stays usable and
install only after an explicit Restart tap. A maintainer can still force a
blocking update for one release by setting priority 4-5 in the Play Console;
the app reads that value from `serverPriority` on each check. Flexible-first
depends on `serverPriority` being returned by the patched bridge, so the adapter
tests pin normal and urgent priorities.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep immediate-first from ADR 0031:** rejected; it hides the flexible path
  on every device where Play allows immediate updates.
- **Always flexible, ignoring priority:** rejected; it removes the Play Console
  emergency lever without an app-side replacement.
- **App-side forced-update policy:** rejected for now; the existing store
  priority is already the configured signal.

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Add or update tests.

# ADR 0037: Per-agent model memory and explicit auto-model thinking levels

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-05
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: —
- Related: [Auto model routing](../product/auto-model-routing.md), [Chat components](../design/components/chat.md), [Onboarding components](../design/components/onboarding.md)

## Context

Chat stored one server-scoped `modelId` for every agent. Switching from Build to
Plan therefore reused Build's model, and onboarding asked for a global default
before the user had seen how agents differ. Model variants (thinking levels)
were selectable in the composer, but auto-model tiers could only choose a model,
not the level used when routing to that model.

## Decision

`ChatPreferences.agentModelSelections` stores the latest model ID per agent.
Selecting a model writes the current agent's entry; switching agents resolves
that agent's entry. An agent without an entry sends no explicit model so the
server/agent default applies. Existing `modelId` values are migrated once to the
current agent.

Auto-model tiers keep their model preference and gain
`tierVariants: Record<'simple' | 'standard' | 'complex', string | null>`. A valid
tier variant overrides the per-model variant for routed sends; an unsupported
value falls back to `modelVariantSelections` or the model default without
blocking routing.

Both maps are server-scoped through the workspace registry and saved connection
profiles. Onboarding no longer writes a default model.

## Consequences

Switching agents restores the expected model and sending with an unconfigured
agent keeps the server default. Users who relied on one global default get that
model assigned to the agent that was active during the upgrade.

Model catalogs can be temporarily incomplete; stored IDs remain in preferences
and are validated at send time. Agent-specific variants are not stored; thinking
levels remain per model plus the optional auto-tier override.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep one global model:** rejected; it breaks the agent workflow the composer
  already exposes.
- **Store full provider/model/variant objects per agent:** rejected; model IDs
  already include the provider, and variants have an existing per-model map.
- **Force a default model during onboarding:** rejected; the server already has
  an agent/config default, and the choice belongs in the composer per agent.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Add or update tests.
- [ ] Link this ADR from the change summary.

# ADR 0038: One archived-projects switch in the project picker

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-11-06
- Deciders: maintainers
- Supersedes: [ADR 0034](0034-device-local-project-archive.md)
- Related: [Functional specification](../product/functional-spec.md#2-pick-a-project), [State and data](../architecture/state-and-data.md#projects), [Chat components](../design/components/chat.md), [Screen components](../design/components/screens.md)

## Context

ADR 0034 added device-local hidden projects as a collapsed section that search
expanded, while ADR 0030 kept server-archived projects behind a separate switch
lower in the picker. The two controls made archive discovery unpredictable:
search could bypass the local switch, and the server switch sat after the whole
project list. The picker also scrolled the Add project action away with the
list.

## Decision

The project picker exposes one Show archived projects switch directly below its
search and server filters. It starts off on every open and reveals both archive
sources:

- device-local hidden rows under "Archived on this device (N)" with Restore;
- V2 server-archived rows under "Archived on OpenCode" with Restore.

Neither section is collapsible. Search filters the rows that the switch already
reveals; it no longer expands hidden rows on its own. The project list scrolls
internally, while the filters and switch stay fixed above it and Add project
stays pinned below it.

The hidden-project persistence, connection scoping, stale-marker behavior and
active-project fallback from ADR 0034 are unchanged.

## Consequences

Users have one predictable place to find both archive kinds. The local and
server sections stay visibly distinct because their restore semantics differ.
Because search no longer bypasses the switch, a hidden project is not found by
typing alone; the user must turn the switch on. The picker layout no longer
scrolls its primary add action out of view.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep two archive controls:** rejected because the local section and server
  switch were easy to miss and behaved differently.
- **Merge local and server archived rows into one list:** rejected because local
  restore updates only the device marker, while server restore calls
  `location.get` and invalidates the shared catalog; one list would blur that
  difference.
- **Keep search auto-expanding local hidden rows:** rejected because it bypassed
  the switch and made visibility depend on the query.

## Follow-up

- [x] Update the affected implementation docs.
- [x] Update the owning projects E2E flow.
