# Plugin GUIs

Back to the [architecture index](README.md). Decision:
[ADR 0027](../adr/0027-sandboxed-mobile-plugin-gui-host.md).

OpenCode V2 plugins may ship a `./gui-experimental` CommonJS bundle. The mobile
app loads that bundle into an Expo DOM WebView and mounts its first `Panel`.
There is no per-plugin code in the app: discovery, loading and rendering are
generic.

## Transport and loading

1. The Extensions plugin tab lists active plugins whose `features.gui` is true.
2. `GET /api/plugin/gui?id=<id>&location[directory]=…` returns
   `{ code, revision, options }`. The app uses the connection's authenticated
   fetch pipeline (`features/extensions/services/plugin-gui-service.ts`).
3. `features/extensions/ui/plugin-gui-loader.ts` evaluates the bundle with a
   local `require` map. `plugin-gui-modules.ts` provides `solid-js`,
   `solid-js/web`, `solid-js/store`, the local SDK shim, RPC tokens and file,
   review and browser contract tokens. Unknown modules fail closed; Electron
   and Node built-ins are inert placeholders.
4. `plugin-gui-sdk.ts` provides `Plugin.define`, registries, contracts, stores,
   `usePlugin`, `usePanel`, `bindPlugin`, `createKeyed`, `createLatest` and
   `createVisitState` for the WebView.
5. `plugin-gui-runtime.ts` creates a Shadow DOM root, provides `ctx`, runs the
   window `setup`, injects `Style` into the shadow root and renders the first
   panel with `solid-js/web`.

The published `@opencode/plugin` package currently blocks its host entrypoint
(`./gui/host`), so the loader and SDK shim live in this feature. They mirror the
documented window contract, not the desktop host implementation.

## Supported profile

`MOBILE_GUI_API = 1` supports:

- identity, options, app metadata, signal, `t`, `plural` (both `{name}` and
  `{{name}}` placeholders), `add`, `list`;
- sessions (current), servers (the active connection), RPC and current-session
  reads, tabs (single session route), layout (full-screen panel), storage and
  declared stores, dialogs (`confirm`, `alert`, `prompt`, `select`), toasts,
  attention as an in-view toast, system copy/save/openExternal, locale,
  appearance, router and workspace events;
- `Panel`, `Command`, `MenuItem` and `Style` registries, plus a small DOM
  `ctx.ui` kit.

Unsupported or inactive: `ctx.main`/Ipc, `ctx.embeds`, `ctx.desktop`, native
menus, function-valued contracts across plugins, `ctx.dialogs.open` and native
`ctx.ui` components. A plugin that requires one of these fails closed or shows
an unavailable state; it is never half-registered as a native surface.

Known limits of this first profile:

- RPC events are not pushed into the WebView; plugins that only listen for
  events must poll, as flowgraph does.
- `ctx.storage` and declared stores are in-memory for the lifetime of the panel.
- `ctx.screen` is undefined; composer and file-tree APIs are not exposed.
- `ctx.layout` is a full-screen panel, not a side region or a session tab strip.
- The host renders one panel at a time. When a plugin contributes more than
  one panel, the screen shows a panel switcher and defaults to the first.

## Security boundary

Plugin panels are available on Android and iOS. Web builds hide the launcher
and show the unavailable state on the direct route. Expo renders DOM components
in the app page on web, where the native WebView boundary is absent.

- Plugin code runs in a WebView, never in the React Native realm.
- The WebView receives no server credential. `ctx.client.rpc` and
  `session.get` call native callbacks; an RPC id is allowed only when every
  word in it also appears in the plugin id or package source (so
  `@slkiser/opencode-quota.server` may call `slkiser.opencode-quota`), and
  session reads are restricted to the routed session.
- Direct `fetch`, XHR, WebSocket, EventSource, `sendBeacon` and `window.open`
  are blocked best-effort before the bundle evaluates. This is not a process
  sandbox; a sandboxed iframe with CSP is the follow-up.
- `Style` is injected into a Shadow DOM root, not the app document.
- External URLs are limited to http(s)/mailto; plugin toasts and dialogs render
  inside the host chrome.

## UI

- A puzzle button appears in the chat header, between New chat and Usage,
  whenever the connection has at least one active plugin advertising a GUI
  (`features.gui`). It is not gated on the selected session, so it shows on
  every chat — including a brand-new empty one — on that connection. Pressing it
  opens the active plugin GUI directly; there is no separate chooser sheet. The
  button is absent while the list is loading or empty. The list stays observed
  for the active workspace and is refetched on plugin/config/command updates, so
  a location that is still booting cannot leave an empty list cached and hide
  the button.
- When several plugins contribute GUIs, a dropdown at the top of the overlay
  selects the active plugin. The selection is remembered in the workspace
  runtime for the app session, so navigating between chats keeps it; it resets
  on relaunch. If the remembered plugin is unavailable, the first plugin in the
  server list is used. With no earlier choice, the first plugin is the default.
- The active plugin renders in a large bottom overlay (about 72% of the
  window) with the host header and WebView. The overlay closes with Back, Close
  or the host's close action.
- When a plugin contributes more than one panel, a dropdown at the top of the
  overlay selects the visualization; the first panel is the default.
- Settings → Extensions still owns plugin installation and removal. GUI launch
  is intentionally in the chat header, not Settings. The standalone
  `/plugin?id=<id>&session=<id>` route remains a deep-link fallback.
- `ctx.tabs.open` and the panel session button use in-app workspace navigation
  (`openSessionInProject`) with the current session directory, not the external
  `/session/<id>` deep link, so the project context is preserved. Failures stay
  in the panel error state.
- With no session selected the overlay falls back to the connection directory,
  so globally installed plugins still render and can offer their own
  run/session picker.
- `Panel.mobile` is used as the panel title; `Panel.list` receives the panel id
  in `open`, so a plugin's own stored-tab logic still works.

## Validation

- `features/extensions/__tests__/plugin-gui-loader.test.ts` covers CJS default
  exports, main-only plugins, missing setup, newer API versions and unknown
  modules.
- A local Playwright harness evaluates the real flowgraph 0.6.0 bundle, runs its
  setup, renders mermaid, opens a session from a graph node and shows its cancel
  dialog. This is the device-independent smoke check for the host contract.
- Device validation is still required for WebView lifecycle, memory, keyboard,
  safe areas and accessibility.

## Agent preference reconciliation

After preference hydration, the AI capability owner validates the stored agent
against the eligible primary catalog. It retains a valid user choice, otherwise
uses the eligible configured `default_agent`, Build, or first eligible server
entry. Project/server changes and late preference hydration revalidate the choice;
stale clients cannot write it. Empty catalogs and catalogs without an eligible
replacement preserve stored preferences and expose no effective selection.
Execution resolves the same choice independently of the effect.

Capability snapshots retain agent mode/hidden and the configured default. Older
snapshots remain readable without guessing missing metadata; live discovery
restores eligibility when available. See [ADR 0026](../adr/0026-metadata-driven-agent-selection.md).

# Storybook

Storybook is the review catalog for reusable presentation components. It runs on
the web through `react-native-web` and renders the production components with
the real appearance provider and Uniwind theme. The decorator supplies a static
UpdatesContext fixture for interaction blockers; it runs no update orchestration.

It is a development tool. It is not part of the app bundle, the E2E export, or
the release artifacts.

## Run

```bash
npm run storybook        # http://localhost:6006
npm run build:storybook  # static build check, output in storybook-static/
```

`storybook-static/` is generated and gitignored. Run the build check when you
change a story, a shared component used by a story, or the Storybook config. CI
runs the same build in the `ci.yml` static job.

## Configuration

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `.storybook/main.ts` | Story globs, addons, `react-native` → `react-native-web` aliasing, web extension resolution |
| `.storybook/preview.tsx` | Appearance provider, Uniwind theme, i18n, light/dark and accent toolbar controls |
| `.storybook/stubs/vector-icons.tsx` | Placeholder icon component because Expo icon fonts are not loaded on web |
| `.storybook/stories/` | Cross-cutting stories such as design foundations |

The Vite pre-transform also resolves provider PNG requires to asset imports and
omits Expo’s declarations-only global module so the production model picker
can render its real web image implementation.

Stories are co-located with components:

```text
shared/ui/text-field.tsx
shared/ui/text-field.stories.tsx
shared/ui/settings/setting-rows.tsx
shared/ui/settings/setting-rows.stories.tsx
```

## What belongs

Add a story when a component is reusable or shared:

- primitives in `shared/ui/`
- shared settings controls in `features/settings/ui/sections/`
- reusable feedback/status components
- foundations such as palette, spacing, shape, and typography

A story should:

- import the production component, never a copy
- render meaningful props and states: default, disabled, error, loading, long
  values, narrow width, and destructive where relevant
- use the preview decorators for theme and shared UI; do not wrap it in a parallel
  visual system
- use localized strings or stable story-only labels; do not hard-code product
  copy that must be translated
- remain deterministic; no network, timers, or real native modules

## What does not belong

- full screens or route controllers
- provider orchestration, connection setup, or session state
- components that require a real native module, camera, microphone, store,
  Bluetooth, or a physical device
- stories that duplicate E2E coverage instead of isolating a presentation state

Provider-coupled surfaces are covered by Playwright flows. If a shared component
needs a provider only for a palette or theme, use the existing preview decorator
instead of adding a new mock.

## Adding a story

1. Put the story next to the component as `<component>.stories.tsx`.
2. Use CSF 3 with `Meta` and `StoryObj` from `@storybook/react-vite`.
3. Give it a stable `title` under `Foundations/`, `Controls/`, `Feedback/`, or
   the matching surface.
4. Cover the states a reviewer cannot easily reach in the app.
5. Run `npm run build:storybook`.
6. If the component has a visual contract, link the story from the
   [component inventory](component-inventory.md) or the change summary.

Example:

```tsx
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite';
import { TextField } from './text-field';

const meta = {
  title: 'Controls/Text input',
  component: TextField,
  args: { label: 'Server URL' },
} satisfies Meta<typeof TextField>;

export default meta;
type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>;

export const Default: Story = {};
export const Error: Story = { args: { invalid: true, value: 'invalid' } };
```

## Review checklist

- Light and dark scheme
- Every accent preset when color is part of the contract
- Disabled, error, loading, and empty states where applicable
- Long labels, long values, and 320-point width
- Keyboard focus and accessible name/state
- No horizontal overflow
- No network or native dependency

## Limitations

- The web preview does not prove native gestures, keyboard behavior, safe areas,
  screen-reader output, or native module behavior.
- Icon fonts are replaced by a placeholder in the web catalog. This is a
  Storybook-only shim; production icons are unchanged.
- A component that cannot be isolated without a large provider mock should stay
  in E2E coverage rather than gaining a fragile story.
- Overlay and selection stories run the production web primitives, appearance, safe areas and portal host. Native gestures and window behavior still require device validation.

# Development

OpenCode Mobile is built with Expo and React Native.

### Requirements

- Node.js 22.13+ (the range in `package.json` `engines` is authoritative; `.nvmrc` pins 22)
- npm
- Android Studio / Xcode for native builds

The unit suite runs under Vitest 5, which requires Node `^22.12.0 || ^24.0.0 || >=26.0.0`. Older Node versions will fail to start the test runner.

> If the working tree lives on a shared or network drive, macOS may leave `._*` AppleDouble sidecar files behind. They are gitignored, but delete them before copying the tree to a build/test mirror so they never reach a bundle or native project.

### Getting Started

1. Clone the repository and install dependencies:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/alvarolorentedev/opencode-mobile.git
   cd opencode-mobile
   npm install
   ```

2. Start the development server:
   ```bash
   npm run start
   ```

3. For a development client build:
   ```bash
   npm run start:dev-client
   ```

   Native Cloud Link is available in every build. Purchase/Restore requires a native
   development or store build, not Expo Go. Use
   `EXPO_APP_VARIANT=development npm run start:dev-client` for the separate dev app.
   Cloud Link routes real purchases to `https://api.opencodecloud.link` and test purchases
   to `https://apistaging.opencodecloud.link` automatically. No manual URL configuration
   is needed. The resolved environment survives relaunch. Products come from its backend catalog,
   never app configuration. See [Cloud Link prerequisites and validation](../product/cloud-link.md).

### Optional local agent tooling

Expo publishes official AI agent skills for generic Expo and React Native work
(`npx skills add expo/skills --global --agent codex`, or the official Expo plugin for Claude Code / Codex). They
complement this repository's `AGENTS.md`, design system, and fake-server

- Static release verification covers signing, package identity, version, ABI, native libraries, R8/ProGuard safety, the WorkManager constructor, FOSS exclusions and 16 KB page-size alignment. It cannot guarantee successful device startup; Google Play internal testing and TestFlight are the real-device validation environments
- See [Android Build / Release Notes](./integrations-and-operations.md#release-abi-and-16-kb-page-size)

### In-app update priority

Normal release (flexible, the default):

1. Bump `version`, `android.versionCode` and `ios.buildNumber`, update the Play changelog, commit and push to `main`.
2. Push the `v<version>` tag. `release.yml` publishes with priority `0`: the app downloads in the background and shows its own restart toast.

Emergency release (immediate):

1. Complete the normal release steps, then push the tag and cancel the automatic run before its `distribute-play` job if you need to publish with priority instead.
2. Run the `Release` workflow manually for that tag with `update_priority` `4` or `5`. Play then requires its full-screen update flow for users below that version.

Priority is per release, not per app: Google Play cannot change it after the release is rolled out, and a device may observe the highest priority across skipped versions and other tracks. A priority of `4`–`5` therefore affects devices that jump from any older version, even if an intermediate release was normal. Do not use `4`–`5` for routine releases. This is Google Play's in-app update priority, unrelated to notification priority or the version number.

## 14. Project archive is server-automatic

OpenCode archives a project when every known directory has been missing for an
hour, and resolving the directory again unarchives it. The V2 protocol exposes
no request that archives or deletes a project on demand: `project.update`
accepts canonical, name, icon, and commands only. The picker therefore treats
archived projects as a read-only server state behind a toggle and offers
restore, not archive. A separate device-local "Archived on this device" marker
can hide a server project from this picker and restore it, but it never changes
the server catalog and is not a server archive.

Exit plan:

- If the server adds a project archive/delete endpoint, add it to the V2 client
  and map the picker action to it with the same destructive confirmation and
  invalidation as the other project mutations.
- Do not emulate archive by editing the canonical directory or deleting files.

# Auto Model Routing

Auto model routing classifies each prompt into `simple`, `standard`, or
`complex` and selects a model from the enabled model catalog before submission.
It is opt-in and never falls back to a heuristic classifier.

## Classifiers

Two classifiers are supported. Neither one guesses a tier.

### On-device

- Runtime: `llama.rn` (llama.cpp) with a pinned GGUF pack.
- Pack: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct Q4_K_M, Apache-2.0, approximately 491 MB.
- The pack is downloaded only after an explicit action and is never bundled in
  the app binary.
- Output is constrained with the GBNF grammar
  `root ::= "simple" | "standard" | "complex"`.
- The runtime uses a 2,048-token context, four threads, CPU inference, and
  releases the model after five minutes idle or when the app backgrounds.
- If the pack is missing, removed, or fails to load, on-device routing is
  disabled. The send uses the user's normal default model.

- Request: `POST /api/experimental/generate/text` with the classifier prompt a

- OpenCode classification sends the classifier prompt to the selected model on

The deterministic backend lives under `tests/fake-opencode/`. It is the
behavioral contract for the app, not a mock of individual functions.

- `tests/fake-opencode/server-v1.mjs` emulates the OpenCode 1.x contract.

Both servers raise `keepAliveTimeout` above a single flow's duration. Playwright's
`APIRequestContext` pools keep-alive sockets per test, and Node's 5s default
could close an idle connection between a long UI step and the next control
request, which surfaced as an intermittent `apiRequestContext ... socket hang
up` failure. The test runner owns the process lifetime, so the longer tim

nd waits for client approval before finishing.

### Question Scenario

The server emits a pending assistant question and waits for an ordered answer payload before finishing.

### Stream Disconnect Scenario

The SSE endpoint intentionally fails, forcing the app to complete the workflow through polling fallback.

### Provider Retry Scenario (V2)

A prompt fails mid-turn (`session.execution.failed`) and the server schedules an automatic retry (`session.retry.scheduled`). The retry status is event-only: the running set excludes it, so a session-list refresh must preserve it. The recovered output is then written to state with no SSE event, so only the busy safety poll can surface it. This reproduces the Android freeze from issue #71.

OpenCode Mobile is an independent, community-built mobile companion for OpenCode. It connects to the OpenCode server you already run and gives you a focused control surface when you are away from your desk.

This F-Droid build connects only to OpenCode servers that you host or control. Your source code stays on your OpenCode host; the app talks to infrastructure you choose.

What you can do:
- Start and continue coding sessions, picking an agent and model
- Watch agent progress instead of waiting for a generic notification
- Review and approve permission requests
- Manage workspaces, sessions, servers, and model selection
- Use the terminal for focused commands
- Browse and patch project files
- Dictate prompts with voice input
- Inspect context utilization, token activity, and estimated cost

How it works:
Your phone connects over HTTPS to an OpenCode server that you expose through a secure tunnel, VPN, or reverse proxy. OpenCode and its trademarks belong to their respective owners.

F-Droid build notes:
This build is produced without proprietary Google libraries. It excludes Google Play Billing and the ML Kit barcode scanner, so the optional paid Cloud Link subscription and its QR pairing are not available. It also compiles expo-notifications against free replacement classes instead of Firebase Cloud Messaging; local task-completion notifications still work. To connect, enter your OpenCode server URL and credentials manually.

Voice input uses the speech recognizer installed on your device. If on-device recognition fails, the recognizer may send audio to its provider for network recognition. You can use typed prompts without enabling voice input.
